sources.title: Samsung readies $648 billion bet, report says, as AI boom reshapes South Korea - Yahoo Finance
passages: SEOUL, June 26 (Reuters) - Samsung Group will unveil a sweeping decade-long investment plan on Monday, pledging 1,000 trillion won ($648 billion) to anchor South Korea's next growth cycle, ‌including a possible 300 trillion won push to build chip factories in the country's southwest, a media report ‌said.

At its core, the initiative appears designed to decentralise South Korea's AI boom ‌into a nationwide engine of growth, easing infrastructure ⁠bottlenecks while jumpstarting jobs, innovation hubs and next-generation manufacturing across underserved regions.

The regional politics ​surrounding semiconductor investment became a flashpoint ahead of South ​Korea's June 3 local elections, and debate over where the next wave of funding should go ‌has intensified as Lee's government has made AI a ​core economic policy priority.
Candidates across multiple regions aggressively pitched their areas as the next semiconductor hub, promising to lure giants such as ​Samsung and SK Hynix.

Presidential policy adviser Kim Yong-beom said on Wednesday that SK Hynix and Samsung may need to accelerate projects originally slated for the 2040s into the mid-2030s because AI-driven ‌memory demand was growing faster than expected, leaving no room, power ​or water in the capital region for subsequent expansion.

extraction.body: SEOUL, June 26 (Reuters) - Samsung Group will unveil a sweeping decade-long investment plan on Monday, pledging 1,000 trillion won ($648 billion) to anchor South Korea's next growth cycle, ‌including a possible 300 trillion won push to build chip factories in the country's southwest, a media report ‌said. The investment, which would include AI data centers, batteries and displays, will be announced at a meeting with President Lee Jae Myung at the presidential ​office, the Maeil Business Newspaper said on Friday, without citing sources. Top executives from heavyweights including Samsung Electronics and its rival SK Hynix will attend the meeting and lay out investment plans targeting regions beyond Seoul and its surrounding hubs, the report said. The report did not say when the investment would be made. At its core, the initiative appears designed to decentralise South Korea's AI boom ‌into a nationwide engine of growth, easing infrastructure ⁠bottlenecks while jumpstarting jobs, innovation hubs and next-generation manufacturing across underserved regions. The concentration of the chipmakers' production facilities in areas around Seoul has long drawn political pressure, and has been amplified by ⁠Lee's push for balanced regional development. Lee had separate meetings with the heads of Samsung and SK this week, media reports said. The presidential office said it will announce on Monday "three mega-projects" to drive a national leap forward, although it has not yet confirmed the content ​of ​the projects. Samsung Group is South ​Korea's biggest conglomerate, with chip giant Samsung Electronics as ‌its crown jewel, but also other affiliates such as battery maker Samsung SDI and IT services company Samsung SDS. A presidential adviser said this week that it is in talks with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix on the next phase of large-scale investments in semiconductor production facilities to meet exponential growth in AI-driven demand for chips. Presidential policy adviser Kim Yong-beom said on Wednesday that SK Hynix and Samsung may need to accelerate projects originally slated for the 2040s into the mid-2030s because AI-driven ‌memory demand was growing faster than expected, leaving no room, power ​or water in the capital region for subsequent expansion. The regional politics ​surrounding semiconductor investment became a flashpoint ahead of South ​Korea's June 3 local elections, and debate over where the next wave of funding should go ‌has intensified as Lee's government has made AI a ​core economic policy priority. Lee's approval ​rating has fallen to 51%, the lowest since his inauguration in June last year, Gallup Korea said on Friday. Candidates across multiple regions aggressively pitched their areas as the next semiconductor hub, promising to lure giants such as ​Samsung and SK Hynix. Proposals ranged from ‌a 500 trillion won chip complex in the southwest to expanded clusters in Gyeonggi, Chungcheong and Gangwon, according ​to local media, underscoring a nationwide contest for strategic tech investment.

passages: Electronics giant Samsung says it plans to invest around 300tn won ($230.8bn; £189.6bn) over 20 years in the South Korea government's push to develop a mega semiconductor hub in the country.

South Korea is home to other major microprocessor manufacturers such as SK Hynix.
This will be put towards building five chip factories, the firm told the BBC.
Samsung is the world's biggest maker of memory chips, smartphones and TVs.

This will be put towards building five chip factories, the firm told the BBC. Samsung is the world's biggest maker of memory chips, smartphones and TVs. Under the official plan, companies in high-tech industries will be offered incentives like expanded tax breaks and infrastructure support. "The mega cluster will be the key base of our semiconductor ecosystem," South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy said in a statement on Wednesday . It said it planned to secure around 550tn won in private-sector investment and "leap forward as a leading country in the middle of fierce global competition over advanced industries". South Korea's move comes as "major players are ramping up efforts to boost onshore manufacturing in the semiconductor sector," Paul Triolo from the global advisory firm Albright Stonebridge Group told the BBC. "It wants to emulate to some degree Taiwan's clustering effect, where the trifecta of science parks... form a massive cluster that has attracted numerous other companies, both upstream and downstream in the supply chain," he said. Semiconductors, which power everything from mobile phones to military hardware, are at the centre of a bitter dispute between the US and China. Around the same time, South Korea's trade ministry raised concerns over the US policy on semiconductors. The ministry said the Chips Act "could deepen business uncertainties, violate companies' management and technology rights as well as make the United States less attractive as an investment option". The South Korean government has greenlit the Yongin Semiconductor National Industrial Complex three months earlier than expected, which will significantly reduce the project planning timeline, reports BusinessKorea . The science park is said to be the world's largest semiconductor hub, accommodating multiple fabs, power plants, and fab suppliers. The Yongin Semiconductor National Industrial Complex spans 7.28 square kilometers (equivalent to 1,020 soccer fields or 3.6 times the size of Monaco, or about half the size of Beverly Hills). It will feature six major semiconductor fabrication plants, three power plants, and 60 small and medium-sized enterprises specializing in materials, parts, and equipment necessary to keep the fabs operating. The first semiconductor plant in YSNIC is expected to begin operations by 2030. Bringing together major makers of microelectronics — such as Samsung and SK hynix — and their suppliers in one large Yongin Semiconductor Cluster is a smart move from the South Korean government as it will enable close collaboration between chipmakers and their suppliers, which might speed up the development of new process technologies and/or shrinking time-to-yield. The report says that the Yongin Cluster complex aims to attract private investments totaling 300 trillion won ($203.75 billion), generate an estimated 1.6 million jobs, and add 700 trillion won ($475.41 billion) in production value once completed. ConstructionThe construction of the Yongin Cluster, initially planned for 2029, will begin in December 2026, a leap forward of three and a half years. To do so, the Korean government expedited land compensation processes, which are set to start next year, and intends to expand critical infrastructure like roads, water, and electricity as soon as possible. In addition to its industrial scope, the complex will include residential areas, creating a small mixed-use city. The approval ceremony occurred at Samsung Electronics' Giheung Campus in Gyeonggi Province on December 26. The event brought together key participants, including Samsung Electronics and SK hynix and representatives from the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, and Transport, Gyeonggi Province, Yongin City, Korea Land and Housing Corporation (LH). During the gathering, officials unveiled a detailed development blueprint for the Yongin Semiconductor National Industrial Complex to highlight the government's dedication to advancing the country's semiconductor sector. sources.title: A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub
passages: Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor.
To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea.
Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online.
Along with the cautionary messages, there’s a sense of urgency in the air.

And for years the company watched its domestic rival SK Hynix pull ahead in the global market for the high-bandwidth models that power Nvidia’s AI accelerators. (Meanwhile, the Taiwanese chipmaker TSMC has dominated the foundry business, manufacturing chips that other companies design.) The Pyeongtaek build-out is Samsung’s attempt to reclaim its lead on memory chips.
It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex.
Thousands of workers, dressed head to toe in black with sky-blue vests, take off helmets bearing their names and fab numbers.
They walk to lunch, sweaty and flushed, in chunky sneakers capped with yellow rubber toe guards.
Some hop on scooters or motorcycles to get around the campus, which covers an area about the size of New York City’s Central Park.
They’ll dine at buffets, diners, and beef stew joints, walking past banners advertising short-term leases for studio apartments.
Some stop by real estate offices to inquire, stepping up to the same counters where Samsung’s salaried engineers buy new homes .

extraction.body: At the world’s biggest chipmaking complex, Samsung is building the fabs it needs for the AI memory boom. Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring. It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex. Thousands of workers, dressed head to toe in black with sky-blue vests, take off helmets bearing their names and fab numbers. They walk to lunch, sweaty and flushed, in chunky sneakers capped with yellow rubber toe guards. Some hop on scooters or motorcycles to get around the campus, which covers an area about the size of New York City’s Central Park. They’ll dine at buffets, diners, and beef stew joints, walking past banners advertising short-term leases for studio apartments. Some stop by real estate offices to inquire, stepping up to the same counters where Samsung’s salaried engineers buy new homes . In front of the fourth fab, I meet Choi Hye-rin, a 35-year-old safety officer, as she wipes her forehead with a handkerchief. At dawn, she boarded one of the shuttle buses that ferry workers in from Songtan, an older, scrappier district. She oversees the safety of a crew responsible for building cable ducts. She writes reports, inspects equipment, and checks the chemicals the workers handle. She’s one of hundreds of women working on site, many employed as spotters who walk ahead of heavy equipment. Safety is a big deal here. After lunch, construction picks right back up. Excavators move past rust-red steel structures rising high under tower cranes. Banners that hang from the highest girders read, “Even if the work runs late, don’t rush.” A giant LED scoreboard announces the winners of a contest for writing a poem about safety. Helmets stickered with a pledge, “I will not work if it’s not safe,” perch atop lockers. The finished fabs glisten from across the street. Along with the cautionary messages, there’s a sense of urgency in the air. Samsung predicts that demand for memory chips will continue to surge through 2028. And for years the company watched its domestic rival SK Hynix pull ahead in the global market for the high-bandwidth models that power Nvidia’s AI accelerators. (Meanwhile, the Taiwanese chipmaker TSMC has dominated the foundry business, manufacturing chips that other companies design.) The Pyeongtaek build-out is Samsung’s attempt to reclaim its lead on memory chips. Although the heat can be brutal and the work zones are crowded, Hye-rin has no plans to leave. “The rate here is higher than other construction sites, and the work is relatively easy,” she says. She gets paid 140,000 won ($97) a day and expects the boom to keep her busy for some time: “You just keep coming back.” Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

Along with the cautionary messages, there’s a sense of urgency in the air. Samsung predicts that demand for memory chips will continue to surge through 2028. (Meanwhile, the Taiwanese chipmaker TSMC has dominated the foundry business, manufacturing chips that other companies design.) The Pyeongtaek build-out is Samsung’s attempt to reclaim its lead on memory chips.

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

At its core, the initiative appears designed to decentralise South Korea's AI boom ‌into a nationwide engine of growth, easing infrastructure ⁠bottlenecks while jumpstarting jobs, innovation hubs and next-generation manufacturing across underserved regions.

Candidates across multiple regions aggressively pitched their areas as the next semiconductor hub, promising to lure giants such as ​Samsung and SK Hynix.

Presidential policy adviser Kim Yong-beom said on Wednesday that SK Hynix and Samsung may need to accelerate projects originally slated for the 2040s into the mid-2030s because AI-driven ‌memory demand was growing faster than expected, leaving no room, power ​or water in the capital region for subsequent expansion.
Electronics giant Samsung says it plans to invest around 300tn won ($230.8bn; £189.6bn) over 20 years in the South Korea government's push to develop a mega semiconductor hub in the country.
"The mega cluster will be the key base of our semiconductor ecosystem," South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy said in a statement on Wednesday .
South Korea is home to other major microprocessor manufacturers such as SK Hynix.
This will be put towards building five chip factories, the firm told the BBC.
Samsung is the world's biggest maker of memory chips, smartphones and TVs.

The investment, which would include AI data centers, batteries and displays, will be announced at a meeting with President Lee Jae Myung at the presidential ​office, the Maeil Business Newspaper said on Friday, without citing sources. Top executives from heavyweights including Samsung Electronics and its rival SK Hynix will attend the meeting and lay out investment plans targeting regions beyond Seoul and its surrounding hubs, the report said. The report did not say when the investment would be made. At its core, the initiative appears designed to decentralise South Korea's AI boom ‌into a nationwide engine of growth, easing infrastructure ⁠bottlenecks while jumpstarting jobs, innovation hubs and next-generation manufacturing across underserved regions. The concentration of the chipmakers' production facilities in areas around Seoul has long drawn political pressure, and has been amplified by ⁠Lee's push for balanced regional development. Lee had separate meetings with the heads of Samsung and SK this week, media reports said. The presidential office said it will announce on Monday "three mega-projects" to drive a national leap forward, although it has not yet confirmed the content ​of ​the projects. Samsung Group is South ​Korea's biggest conglomerate, with chip giant Samsung Electronics as ‌its crown jewel, but also other affiliates such as battery maker Samsung SDI and IT services company Samsung SDS. A presidential adviser said this week that it is in talks with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix on the next phase of large-scale investments in semiconductor production facilities to meet exponential growth in AI-driven demand for chips. Presidential policy adviser Kim Yong-beom said on Wednesday that SK Hynix and Samsung may need to accelerate projects originally slated for the 2040s into the mid-2030s because AI-driven ‌memory demand was growing faster than expected, leaving no room, power ​or water in the capital region for subsequent expansion. The regional politics ​surrounding semiconductor investment became a flashpoint ahead of South ​Korea's June 3 local elections, and debate over where the next wave of funding should go ‌has intensified as Lee's government has made AI a ​core economic policy priority. Lee's approval ​rating has fallen to 51%, the lowest since his inauguration in June last year, Gallup Korea said on Friday. Candidates across multiple regions aggressively pitched their areas as the next semiconductor hub, promising to lure giants such as ​Samsung and SK Hynix. Proposals ranged from ‌a 500 trillion won chip complex in the southwest to expanded clusters in Gyeonggi, Chungcheong and Gangwon, according ​to local media, underscoring a nationwide contest for strategic tech investment.

extraction.body: Electronics giant Samsung says it plans to invest around 300tn won ($230.8bn; £189.6bn) over 20 years in the South Korea government's push to develop a mega semiconductor hub in the country. This will be put towards building five chip factories, the firm told the BBC. Samsung is the world's biggest maker of memory chips, smartphones and TVs. Under the official plan, companies in high-tech industries will be offered incentives like expanded tax breaks and infrastructure support. "The mega cluster will be the key base of our semiconductor ecosystem," South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy said in a statement on Wednesday . It said it planned to secure around 550tn won in private-sector investment and "leap forward as a leading country in the middle of fierce global competition over advanced industries". South Korea's move comes as "major players are ramping up efforts to boost onshore manufacturing in the semiconductor sector," Paul Triolo from the global advisory firm Albright Stonebridge Group told the BBC. "It wants to emulate to some degree Taiwan's clustering effect, where the trifecta of science parks... form a massive cluster that has attracted numerous other companies, both upstream and downstream in the supply chain," he said. Semiconductors, which power everything from mobile phones to military hardware, are at the centre of a bitter dispute between the US and China. In October, Washington announced that it would require licences for companies exporting chips to China using US tools or software, no matter where they are made in the world. Last week, the Netherlands said it also planned to put restrictions on its "most advanced" microchip technology exports to protect national security. Around the same time, South Korea's trade ministry raised concerns over the US policy on semiconductors. The South Korean government has greenlit the Yongin Semiconductor National Industrial Complex three months earlier than expected, which will significantly reduce the project planning timeline, reports BusinessKorea . The science park is said to be the world's largest semiconductor hub, accommodating multiple fabs, power plants, and fab suppliers. The Yongin Semiconductor National Industrial Complex spans 7.28 square kilometers (equivalent to 1,020 soccer fields or 3.6 times the size of Monaco, or about half the size of Beverly Hills). It will feature six major semiconductor fabrication plants, three power plants, and 60 small and medium-sized enterprises specializing in materials, parts, and equipment necessary to keep the fabs operating. The first semiconductor plant in YSNIC is expected to begin operations by 2030. Bringing together major makers of microelectronics — such as Samsung and SK hynix — and their suppliers in one large Yongin Semiconductor Cluster is a smart move from the South Korean government as it will enable close collaboration between chipmakers and their suppliers, which might speed up the development of new process technologies and/or shrinking time-to-yield. The report says that the Yongin Cluster complex aims to attract private investments totaling 300 trillion won ($203.75 billion), generate an estimated 1.6 million jobs, and add 700 trillion won ($475.41 billion) in production value once completed. ConstructionThe construction of the Yongin Cluster, initially planned for 2029, will begin in December 2026, a leap forward of three and a half years. To do so, the Korean government expedited land compensation processes, which are set to start next year, and intends to expand critical infrastructure like roads, water, and electricity as soon as possible. In addition to its industrial scope, the complex will include residential areas, creating a small mixed-use city. The approval ceremony occurred at Samsung Electronics' Giheung Campus in Gyeonggi Province on December 26. The event brought together key participants, including Samsung Electronics and SK hynix and representatives from the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, and Transport, Gyeonggi Province, Yongin City, Korea Land and Housing Corporation (LH). During the gathering, officials unveiled a detailed development blueprint for the Yongin Semiconductor National Industrial Complex to highlight the government's dedication to advancing the country's semiconductor sector. sources.title: A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub
passages: Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor.
To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea.
Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online.
Along with the cautionary messages, there’s a sense of urgency in the air.

And for years the company watched its domestic rival SK Hynix pull ahead in the global market for the high-bandwidth models that power Nvidia’s AI accelerators. (Meanwhile, the Taiwanese chipmaker TSMC has dominated the foundry business, manufacturing chips that other companies design.) The Pyeongtaek build-out is Samsung’s attempt to reclaim its lead on memory chips.
It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex.
Thousands of workers, dressed head to toe in black with sky-blue vests, take off helmets bearing their names and fab numbers.
They walk to lunch, sweaty and flushed, in chunky sneakers capped with yellow rubber toe guards.
Some hop on scooters or motorcycles to get around the campus, which covers an area about the size of New York City’s Central Park.
They’ll dine at buffets, diners, and beef stew joints, walking past banners advertising short-term leases for studio apartments.
Some stop by real estate offices to inquire, stepping up to the same counters where Samsung’s salaried engineers buy new homes .

extraction.body: At the world’s biggest chipmaking complex, Samsung is building the fabs it needs for the AI memory boom. Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring. It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex. Thousands of workers, dressed head to toe in black with sky-blue vests, take off helmets bearing their names and fab numbers. They walk to lunch, sweaty and flushed, in chunky sneakers capped with yellow rubber toe guards. Some hop on scooters or motorcycles to get around the campus, which covers an area about the size of New York City’s Central Park. They’ll dine at buffets, diners, and beef stew joints, walking past banners advertising short-term leases for studio apartments. Some stop by real estate offices to inquire, stepping up to the same counters where Samsung’s salaried engineers buy new homes . In front of the fourth fab, I meet Choi Hye-rin, a 35-year-old safety officer, as she wipes her forehead with a handkerchief. At dawn, she boarded one of the shuttle buses that ferry workers in from Songtan, an older, scrappier district. She oversees the safety of a crew responsible for building cable ducts. She writes reports, inspects equipment, and checks the chemicals the workers handle. She’s one of hundreds of women working on site, many employed as spotters who walk ahead of heavy equipment. Safety is a big deal here. After lunch, construction picks right back up. Excavators move past rust-red steel structures rising high under tower cranes. Banners that hang from the highest girders read, “Even if the work runs late, don’t rush.” A giant LED scoreboard announces the winners of a contest for writing a poem about safety. Helmets stickered with a pledge, “I will not work if it’s not safe,” perch atop lockers. The finished fabs glisten from across the street. Along with the cautionary messages, there’s a sense of urgency in the air. Samsung predicts that demand for memory chips will continue to surge through 2028. And for years the company watched its domestic rival SK Hynix pull ahead in the global market for the high-bandwidth models that power Nvidia’s AI accelerators. (Meanwhile, the Taiwanese chipmaker TSMC has dominated the foundry business, manufacturing chips that other companies design.) The Pyeongtaek build-out is Samsung’s attempt to reclaim its lead on memory chips. Although the heat can be brutal and the work zones are crowded, Hye-rin has no plans to leave. “The rate here is higher than other construction sites, and the work is relatively easy,” she says. She gets paid 140,000 won ($97) a day and expects the boom to keep her busy for some time: “You just keep coming back.” Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

The chip giant has made championing open-weight models, downloadable models that users can modify and inspect on their own, a key part of its growth strategy. Open models are less expensive to use, giving more organizations the option to use AI services. And the more companies that use AI, the more chips Nvidia can sell in the long run. The company's newest models — Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, and Nemotron Bolt E4B 4GB — are designed to run AI agents on everything from data center systems to desktop computers. Super VL is meant to power agents running across tasks that can take several days or weeks, Nvidia explained in a release. The company says that enterprises can also post-train the model on their own data, better customizing it for their exact needs. Bolt 74B is designed for general agentic tasks, such as navigating web browsers and using apps, while Bolt E4B is designed for physical and conversational agents. While open-weight models generally trail closed models in terms of frontier capabilities, most users don't need such intense firepower for the jobs they need to accomplish. What's more, if a company can run open-weight models on its own hardware, they're more or less free to use. That also offers the dual benefit of lower costs and increased privacy, since companies running their own hardware don't have to upload their data to third-party servers. China currently dominates the conversation on open models, with companies including Moonshot AI, Alibaba Cloud ( BABA ), and others offering popular model families such as Kimi K3 and Qwen. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed for US companies to develop and adopt more open-weight models to increase competition in the space and to avoid becoming locked into a system that relies on a small number of closed-weight models. sources.title: Nvidia launches new open models to run agents in the enterprise and on PCs
passages: “Any organization that wants to run agents on Nvidia infrastructure now has an open, optimized model for their tier without having to choose between capability and deployability,” Nvidia’s vice president of Open Models and Software, Kari Briski, wrote in the blog post announcing these models.
The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a large, 120-billion-parameter model geared for agents used by the enterprise.
Nvidia on Thursday launched new open-weight models designed for always-on agents and edge computing.

So, while Nvidia hopes to create a new market for itself selling PCs powered by its chips by creating machines that run the models and agents locally, PC users “can delegate everyday projects … without sending those workloads to the cloud,” Briski wrote.
The GPU giant has an entire family of Nemotron models that do everything from multimodal artificial intelligence to reasoning, coding, math, and enterprise automation.
Nvidia claims that the Super VL completes tasks faster than competing models from Anthropic and OpenAI (Opus 5, GPT 6.1 Sol, Luna, Astra) when post-trained on specific agentic tasks.
These tasks include document intelligence, financial accounting, scientific experimentation, medical insurance claims, and security attack resilience.
While such claims are standard whenever a major tech company announces a new model, Nvidia has backed it up with a list of heavy-hitter companies that it says are using Super VL.
These include Skydance, EY, Ramp, Crowdstrike, Perplexity, and Salesforce .
Super VL and Bolt 74B-A9B are available now, with Bolt E4B coming later this month, Nvidia says.

However, those fast-growing proprietary AI labs are now looking to many other chips and AI system makers beyond Nvidia to power their needs, like AWS’s Trainium and Cerebras, as well as building their own home-grown chips.

The companies’ joint paper identified 30 risk types across five categories and advised enterprises to verify model provenance, test configurations, and reassess risks after material changes, while stating, “Weight openness alone does not determine an AI system’s risk.” A security risk framework lists 30 risk types across five categories Michael Scovetta, Partner Security Assurance Manager at Microsoft, said, “Weight openness alone does not determine an AI system’s risk,” and he added that “Open- and closed-weight models can share many of the same underlying risks, but how those risks materialize depends on the deployment.” The guidance also warned that open-weight models can be fine-tuned, merged, modified, or repackaged, and it cautioned that “Safety behaviors are often the more fragile of the two,” as changes can degrade safeguards while leaving task performance intact. Microsoft and Nvidia recommended using cryptographic signatures to verify that a model matches the publisher’s original artifact, and they advised that “No volume of behavioral testing establishes what an artifact is, only how it behaves.” The guidance said that where signatures are unavailable, organizations should record the unverified integrity as an open risk rather than treating evaluation results as closing it, and it urged monitoring model inputs, outputs, and tool use after deployment. extraction.body: NVIDIA today released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open 120-billion-parameter model that delivers the fastest task completion and highest accuracy for specialized always-on agents. Joining it are two new edge models: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, optimized to balance intelligence and speed per GB for local agentic workloads, and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, optimized for intelligence per GB for fast conversational agents. Super VL and Bolt 74B-A9B are available now, with Bolt E4B coming Oct. 23. The three open models together cover the full range of agent deployments, from large enterprise servers down to edge devices and local hardware. Any organization that wants to run agents on NVIDIA infrastructure now has an open, optimized model for their tier, without having to choose between capability and deployability. Super VL and Bolt join the Nemotron family alongside Lightning and Ultra. Lightning, released in August, handles high-throughput workloads; Ultra handles the hardest reasoning tasks; and Bolt brings intelligence to the edge. Super VL, built in collaboration with the Nemotron Coalition , delivers leading accuracy on multimodal agentic tasks — instruction following, tool use, multistep business workflows, and visual understanding — comparable with NVIDIA’s largest reasoning model at roughly one-fifth the parameter count. As the fastest open agentic model in its class — 5x faster than the next best — it helps enterprise agents complete high-volume tasks faster across workflows that span days or weeks. Unlike closed frontier models, organizations can post-train Super VL on their own data, deploy it on their own infrastructure and oversee what they build. Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is designed to run everyday agentic tasks locally on NVIDIA RTX/DGX Spark, using a native 2-bit quantization to fit in 24GB of memory and run alongside other applications. With Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, users can delegate their projects to popular local agent harnesses — from researching the web to writing to debugging code — all without sending those workloads to the cloud. It is the #1 open model in its class on PinchBench , and the #2 open model for BrowseComp . Bolt E4B 4GB is built for physical and conversational agents on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. It combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power fast local voice assistants, interactive characters and embedded interfaces. Dozens of organizations across industries are post-training Super VL on their own data, tools, policies and workflows to push accuracy higher on the specialized tasks that define their agent deployments. Super VL is being post-trained and customized by organizations across industries. Scale AI post-trained the model for Skydance’s vendor credit finance agent and for EY’s M&A due diligence agent. AfterQuery customized the model for Hebbia for credit agreement analysis. AI21 and Alice post-trained the model for cybersecurity attack resilience. Mercor post-trained the model on APEX-SWE coding benchmark, for coding agents that plan, write and debug code. ModelScope enables developers to fine-tune the model through its ms-swift framework for specialized multimodal applications. Additional organizations customizing Nemotron 3.5 Super VL include Ramp for financial document intelligence; Dream , sovereign AI-powered cybersecurity research and vulnerability analysis; Lila Sciences for scientific discovery and search, and R1 for medical claims analysis and revenue cycle management. TrainLoop post-trained the model with dermatology data from Nolla, which just became the first company approved for AI to write initial patient prescriptions. Software platform companies integrating Nemotron 3.5 Super VL include: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL’s vision language strengths are targeted at what agents encounter in practice: optical character recognition, tables, charts and structured information in visual documents. It processes a web page, extracts text, reads graphs and charts, and returns insights from what it finds. The same applies to PDFs and other documents agents commonly work with. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL understands images, webpages and PDFs and acts on that understanding. Combining text and visual understanding in one model means agents don’t need to route tasks between separate systems — context carries through as work moves from document to data to decision. Openness and customizability reinforce each other. The model ships with open weights, open datasets and training recipes. Control runs in two directions. Organizations can run the model wherever their security and data-residency requirements dictate. They also choose to adopt a model they can adapt, rather than one subject to a provider’s restrictions. Customization is supported through NVIDIA NeMo, Python-based pipelines and open datasets. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL was trained on about 26 trillion tokens across pretraining and continued pretraining, then post-trained with roughly 3.8 million samples and reinforcement learning across dozens of environments. NVIDIA is also releasing open datasets on Hugging Face spanning agentic tool use , finance, instruction following, long context, fairness and vision-language understanding, along with the reinforcement learning environments in NeMo Gym. NVIDIA NIM packages the model as a production-ready microservice with performance-optimized, validated configurations and enterprise-grade support, refreshed every two weeks with security patches and performance improvements. And with the model running on NVIDIA Dynamo, organizations can serve up to 8x more users with 85% lower latency. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is available now on Hugging Face, Open Router, ModelScope community and as NVIDIA NIM. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL runs across NVIDIA’s full hardware stack: on DGX Spark , DGX Station , RTX PRO and RTX systems for local intelligence at the desktop, on NVIDIA Jetson at the edge, and across data center and cloud environments. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24G B is available now on Hugging Face, with support for llama.cpp , Ollama , LM Studio , Unsloth , and vLLM . Built for NVIDIA RTX Spark laptops arriving Oct. 16, it also runs on GeForce RTX PCs , DGX Spark , DGX Station and RTX PRO workstations . Download the open weights , explore customization resources with NVIDIA NeMo, or read the technical blog for the full architecture breakdown. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL’s vision language strengths are targeted at what agents encounter in practice: optical character recognition, tables, charts and structured information in visual documents.

Openness and customizability reinforce each other. The model ships with open weights, open datasets and training recipes.

coreStoryFacts.text: Nvidia ( NVDA ) is expanding its family of open AI models with its latest Nemotron offerings.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Open models are less expensive to use, giving more organizations the option to use AI services.
And the more companies that use AI, the more chips Nvidia can sell in the long run.
Super VL is meant to power agents running across tasks that can take several days or weeks, Nvidia explained in a release.
The company says that enterprises can also post-train the model on their own data, better customizing it for their exact needs.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed for US companies to develop and adopt more open-weight models to increase competition in the space and to avoid becoming locked into a system that relies on a small number of closed-weight models.

“Any organization that wants to run agents on Nvidia infrastructure now has an open, optimized model for their tier without having to choose between capability and deployability,” Nvidia’s vice president of Open Models and Software, Kari Briski, wrote in the blog post announcing these models.
The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a large, 120-billion-parameter model geared for agents used by the enterprise.
Nvidia on Thursday launched new open-weight models designed for always-on agents and edge computing.

So, while Nvidia hopes to create a new market for itself selling PCs powered by its chips by creating machines that run the models and agents locally, PC users “can delegate everyday projects … without sending those workloads to the cloud,” Briski wrote.
The GPU giant has an entire family of Nemotron models that do everything from multimodal artificial intelligence to reasoning, coding, math, and enterprise automation.
Nvidia claims that the Super VL completes tasks faster than competing models from Anthropic and OpenAI (Opus 5, GPT 6.1 Sol, Luna, Astra) when post-trained on specific agentic tasks.
These tasks include document intelligence, financial accounting, scientific experimentation, medical insurance claims, and security attack resilience.
While such claims are standard whenever a major tech company announces a new model, Nvidia has backed it up with a list of heavy-hitter companies that it says are using Super VL.
These include Skydance, EY, Ramp, Crowdstrike, Perplexity, and Salesforce .
Super VL and Bolt 74B-A9B are available now, with Bolt E4B coming later this month, Nvidia says.

However, those fast-growing proprietary AI labs are now looking to many other chips and AI system makers beyond Nvidia to power their needs, like AWS’s Trainium and Cerebras, as well as building their own home-grown chips.
Nvidia launched new open-weight models for agents in enterprises and on PCs, including the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL with 120 billion parameters and two Bolt models intended to run locally.

Nvidia Vice President of Open Models and Software Kari Briski said in a statement, “any organization that wants to run agents on Nvidia’s infrastructure now has an open model that is optimized for its level without having to choose between capacity and deployability.”

Microsoft and Nvidia urged enterprises to assess the security of open-weight AI models throughout deployment, warning that changes to model weights and configurations can weaken safeguards even when a model retains its ability to perform assigned tasks.

The companies’ joint paper identified 30 risk types across five categories and advised enterprises to verify model provenance, test configurations, and reassess risks after material changes, while stating, “Weight openness alone does not determine an AI system’s risk.”

TechCrunch leads with Nvidia’s model launch and deployment, while CSO Online shifts to enterprise risk governance for open-weight adoption.

passages: “Any organization that wants to run agents on Nvidia infrastructure now has an open, optimized model for their tier without having to choose between capability and deployability,” Nvidia’s vice president of Open Models and Software, Kari Briski, wrote in the blog post announcing these models.

Nvidia on Thursday launched new open-weight models designed for always-on agents and edge computing.

So, while Nvidia hopes to create a new market for itself selling PCs powered by its chips by creating machines that run the models and agents locally, PC users “can delegate everyday projects … without sending those workloads to the cloud,” Briski wrote.

Super VL and Bolt 74B-A9B are available now, with Bolt E4B coming later this month, Nvidia says.

However, those fast-growing proprietary AI labs are now looking to many other chips and AI system makers beyond Nvidia to power their needs, like AWS’s Trainium and Cerebras, as well as building their own home-grown chips.

extraction.body: Nvidia on Thursday launched new open-weight models designed for always-on agents and edge computing. The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a large, 120-billion-parameter model geared for agents used by the enterprise. While it uses fewer parameters than the Nemotron 3 Ultra model, Nvidia says it can deliver similar accuracy in instruction-following and tool-use tasks. At the other end of the spectrum, the company also launched two lightweight Bolt models. These are intended to run locally on the new AI PCs (running the Nvidia RTX Spark chip) and workstations running the DGX Spark. Such PCs, aimed at consumers, programmers, and enterprise knowledge workers, are being released right now into the market through partners like Microsoft and Dell. “Any organization that wants to run agents on Nvidia infrastructure now has an open, optimized model for their tier without having to choose between capability and deployability,” Nvidia’s vice president of Open Models and Software, Kari Briski, wrote in the blog post announcing these models. Nvidia claims that the Super VL completes tasks faster than competing models from Anthropic and OpenAI (Opus 5, GPT 6.1 Sol, Luna, Astra) when post-trained on specific agentic tasks. These tasks include document intelligence, financial accounting, scientific experimentation, medical insurance claims, and security attack resilience. While such claims are standard whenever a major tech company announces a new model, Nvidia has backed it up with a list of heavy-hitter companies that it says are using Super VL. These include Skydance, EY, Ramp, Crowdstrike, Perplexity, and Salesforce . Of course, these aren’t the first open-weight models that Nvidia has released that compete with the proprietary frontier labs — companies that are both its customers and its investments. The GPU giant has an entire family of Nemotron models that do everything from multimodal artificial intelligence to reasoning, coding, math, and enterprise automation. However, those fast-growing proprietary AI labs are now looking to many other chips and AI system makers beyond Nvidia to power their needs, like AWS’s Trainium and Cerebras, as well as building their own home-grown chips. So Nvidia is leaning hard into the trend of enterprise companies wanting to run their own open models in their own data centers. “Unlike closed frontier models, organizations can post-train Super VL on their own data, deploy it on their own infrastructure and own what they build,” Briski wrote. But with the announcement or the smaller, local PC models, it is also trying to push forward the nascent trend of consumer AI assistants. While it seems a new AI assistant is introduced every day by startups and Big Tech alike, privacy-weary consumers may not want to invite such agents so deeply into their lives giving them access to info about their families, health, finances, and so on. So, while Nvidia hopes to create a new market for itself selling PCs powered by its chips by creating machines that run the models and agents locally, PC users “can delegate everyday projects … without sending those workloads to the cloud,” Briski wrote. Of the two Bolt models, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is a 74-billion parameter model designed for local agentic tasks. It is intended to balance speed with reasoning to handle multistep reasoning, tool calling, and web browsing. The smallest Bolt E4B is aimed at conversational agents. Super VL and Bolt 74B-A9B are available now, with Bolt E4B coming later this month, Nvidia says. With Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, users can delegate their projects to popular local agent harnesses — from researching the web to writing to debugging code — all without sending those workloads to the cloud. It is the #1 open model in its class on PinchBench , and the #2 open model for BrowseComp . Bolt E4B 4GB is built for physical and conversational agents on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. It combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power fast local voice assistants, interactive characters and embedded interfaces. Dozens of organizations across industries are post-training Super VL on their own data, tools, policies and workflows to push accuracy higher on the specialized tasks that define their agent deployments. AfterQuery customized the model for Hebbia for credit agreement analysis. AI21 and Alice post-trained the model for cybersecurity attack resilience. Mercor post-trained the model on APEX-SWE coding benchmark, for coding agents that plan, write and debug code. ModelScope enables developers to fine-tune the model through its ms-swift framework for specialized multimodal applications. Additional organizations customizing Nemotron 3.5 Super VL include Ramp for financial document intelligence; Dream , sovereign AI-powered cybersecurity research and vulnerability analysis; Lila Sciences for scientific discovery and search, and R1 for medical claims analysis and revenue cycle management. TrainLoop post-trained the model with dermatology data from Nolla, which just became the first company approved for AI to write initial patient prescriptions. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL understands images, webpages and PDFs and acts on that understanding. Combining text and visual understanding in one model means agents don’t need to route tasks between separate systems — context carries through as work moves from document to data to decision. Organizations can run the model wherever their security and data-residency requirements dictate. They also choose to adopt a model they can adapt, rather than one subject to a provider’s restrictions. Customization is supported through NVIDIA NeMo, Python-based pipelines and open datasets. NVIDIA is also releasing open datasets on Hugging Face spanning agentic tool use , finance, instruction following, long context, fairness and vision-language understanding, along with the reinforcement learning environments in NeMo Gym. NVIDIA NIM packages the model as a production-ready microservice with performance-optimized, validated configurations and enterprise-grade support, refreshed every two weeks with security patches and performance improvements. And with the model running on NVIDIA Dynamo, organizations can serve up to 8x more users with 85% lower latency. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is available now on Hugging Face, Open Router, ModelScope community and as NVIDIA NIM. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL runs across NVIDIA’s full hardware stack: on DGX Spark , DGX Station , RTX PRO and RTX systems for local intelligence at the desktop, on NVIDIA Jetson at the edge, and across data center and cloud environments. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24G B is available now on Hugging Face, with support for llama.cpp , Ollama , LM Studio , Unsloth , and vLLM . Built for NVIDIA RTX Spark laptops arriving Oct. 16, it also runs on GeForce RTX PCs , DGX Spark , DGX Station and RTX PRO workstations . Download the open weights , explore customization resources with NVIDIA NeMo, or read the technical blog for the full architecture breakdown. sources.title: Apple teases ‘Pro and Tell’ event for October 28th as touchscreen MacBook Pro anticipation builds - MacDailyNews
passages: Apple marketing chief Greg Joswiak on Monday shared a short teaser video and the message “Can’t wait to pro and tell next week,” confirming the company’s next product experience for Wednesday, October 28th, in Los Angeles.

Gurman has indicated the devices could be introduced around October 28th, with availability potentially following in early November (reports have referenced a possible November 6th window tied to retail preparations).
Earlier speculation about a “MacBook Ultra” name appears to have been walked back, with the touchscreen models expected to remain in the MacBook Pro lineup.
Joswiak’s post, which quickly drew thousands of likes and shares, follows the recent distribution of media invites for an in-person gathering starting at 10 a.m.
• Redesigned 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models with OLED touchscreens (Apple’s first on a Mac), a Dynamic Island cutout replacing the notch, and a significantly lighter design.
These are widely expected to use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips rather than a new M6 Pro/Max generation.
Joswiak’s playful wording and the fluid logo animation have fueled speculation that the teaser alludes to the tactile or visual qualities of the expected OLED touchscreen machines.
The prospect of a touchscreen MacBook Pro represents a significant departure for Apple, which has long argued against touch input on traditional laptops in favor of trackpad and keyboard precision.
This marks Apple’s second hardware-focused experience of the month.
On October 13th in New York, the company introduced the HomeView smart display, HomePod mini 2, and an updated Apple TV 4K under the “Welcome home” banner.
Until then, the combination of confirmed event timing and consistent high-level reporting has set clear expectations for Apple’s next major hardware step.
— Greg Joswiak (@gregjoz) October 19, 2026

The October 28 gathering in Los Angeles is expected to follow a similar hands-on format for select media and creators rather than a traditional livestreamed keynote, with product announcements and videos likely timed to the event. Expected Lineup Centers on Mac and iPad Upgrades While Apple has not confirmed specific products, reporting from Bloomberg News ’ Mark Gurman and coverage across tech outlets points to a Mac- and iPad-focused slate: • Redesigned 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models with OLED touchscreens (Apple’s first on a Mac), a Dynamic Island cutout replacing the notch, and a significantly lighter design. These are widely expected to use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips rather than a new M6 Pro/Max generation. • An entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro and a refreshed iMac powered by the M6 chip, largely retaining current designs. • A new iPad mini with an OLED display, a relocated landscape-oriented FaceTime camera, and an updated speaker system. Gurman has indicated the devices could be introduced around October 28th, with availability potentially following in early November (reports have referenced a possible November 6th window tied to retail preparations). Earlier speculation about a “MacBook Ultra” name appears to have been walked back, with the touchscreen models expected to remain in the MacBook Pro lineup. The prospect of a touchscreen MacBook Pro represents a significant departure for Apple, which has long argued against touch input on traditional laptops in favor of trackpad and keyboard precision. An OLED panel would also mark a display upgrade from the mini-LED technology in recent high-end Pros, promising better contrast, blacks, and brightness alongside the new interaction model and software support (reports have referenced testing with macOS versions that include finger input handling). Joswiak’s playful wording and the fluid logo animation have fueled speculation that the teaser alludes to the tactile or visual qualities of the expected OLED touchscreen machines. The October 28 gathering in Los Angeles is expected to follow a similar hands-on format for select media and creators rather than a traditional livestreamed keynote, with product announcements and videos likely timed to the event.
Expected Lineup Centers on Mac and iPad Upgrades
While Apple has not confirmed specific products, reporting from Bloomberg News ’ Mark Gurman and coverage across tech outlets points to a Mac- and iPad-focused slate:

• Redesigned 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models with OLED touchscreens (Apple’s first on a Mac), a Dynamic Island cutout replacing the notch, and a significantly lighter design. These are widely expected to use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips rather than a new M6 Pro/Max generation.
• An entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro and a refreshed iMac powered by the M6 chip, largely retaining current designs.
• A new iPad mini with an OLED display, a relocated landscape-oriented FaceTime camera, and an updated speaker system.

Gurman has indicated the devices could be introduced around October 28th, with availability potentially following in early November (reports have referenced a possible November 6th window tied to retail preparations). Earlier speculation about a “MacBook Ultra” name appears to have been walked back, with the touchscreen models expected to remain in the MacBook Pro lineup.

The prospect of a touchscreen MacBook Pro represents a significant departure for Apple, which has long argued against touch input on traditional laptops in favor of trackpad and keyboard precision. An OLED panel would also mark a display upgrade from the mini-LED technology in recent high-end Pros, promising better contrast, blacks, and brightness alongside the new interaction model and software support (reports have referenced testing with macOS versions that include finger input handling).

Joswiak’s playful wording and the fluid logo animation have fueled speculation that the teaser alludes to the tactile or visual qualities of the expected OLED touchscreen machines. Apple’s fall product cadence has been busy, following recent iPhone and related launches, and the “Pro and tell” experience appears positioned as a focused showcase for professional and creative users.
Official details will arrive next week. Until then, the combination of confirmed event timing and consistent high-level reporting has set clear expectations for Apple’s next major hardware step.

The iPhone 17e is expected too, packing an A19 chip, MagSafe, and possibly a Dynamic Island—a solid upgrade over the iPhone 16e at the same $599 price.MacBook Pro may get the Pro and Max chip treatmentRounding things out, Apple is widely expected to launch 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.
Apple CEO Tim Cook has confirmed that a wave of product announcements is coming, starting Monday, March 2.

It all starts Monday morning," Cook posted on X, all but confirming what the rumor mill has been churning out for weeks.The company is expected to unveil at least four new products across a three-day stretch, leading up to a hands-on "Apple Experience" event on Wednesday, March 4, in New York, London, and Shanghai.

No design changes are expected — Apple is reportedly saving the big OLED and touchscreen overhaul for the M6 generation later this year.A refreshed Studio Display, new Apple TV, and HomePod mini are also possibilities, though less certain.

sources.title: Agents are your newest insiders. Security must move at their speed. - Microsoft
passages: We introduced Project Perception and the Microsoft cyber stack to help organizations defend with agents.
Today, we are extending Perception to secure the agentic insider .

Guardian Agents help security teams operate continuously, at machine speed and scale, while sensors, context, and actuators across the cyber stack help understand changing agent risk and continuously adapt protection in response.
Agents can be created through Microsoft platforms, integrated through partner platforms and software development kits (SDKs), or introduced locally without a central deployment process.
An agent should not be free to call any tool, API, Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, resource, or other agent it can find.
Local and network and data controls must mediate those paths, observe the calls, and enforce enterprise policy.
Controlling the destination alone is not enough.
Security must also understand the content flowing into and out of the agent, including its sensitivity, provenance, and whether untrusted data may be influencing the agent’s behavior.
Agents are rapidly becoming part of how work gets done.
They can support a range of activities from writing code and researching products to analyzing revenue, processing expenses, and acting across the systems that run the business.
To be most useful, they often need access to company data, applications, tools, and other agents.
That access is what makes agents more capable.

Satya Nadella, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Microsoft, recently described the trust architecture this new era requires: we must separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.
We should not ask a model to be its own security authority.
The controls that determine what it can access, what actions it can take, and whether it should continue operating must sit outside the model, where the model cannot bypass or tamper with them.
The security system must be able to understand what changed and act before a person can manually investigate every signal.
This means an agent can become a policy target even when it was not originally integrated with Microsoft Security.
Sandboxes such as Microsoft Execution Container (MXC) provide policy-controlled access to resources the agent needs to complete its task.
Agents will only be adopted at scale if they can be trusted at scale.
At Microsoft, we are already operating in a world of hundreds of thousands of agents.

As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats.
Those lessons directly inform the innovations we are delivering to help every organization adopt agents with confidence.”
— Terrell Cox, Corporate Vice President (CVP) and Deputy Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), Customer Security, Microsoft
That requires a clear division of responsibility.
Independent controls establish identity, limit privilege, protect data, preserve evidence, and contain unsafe action.
Security continuously reassesses risk and adapts protection as the agent works.
Protect your people, data, and infrastructure with AI-powered, end-to-end security from Microsoft.
Greater model transparency gives security systems deeper evidence to detect suspicious behavior and inform Dynamic Agent Risk.
We have spent decades applying Zero Trust and least privilege to people.
Agents make those principles even more important.
Dynamic Conditional Access extends Microsoft Entra Conditional Access for agents so a change in risk can drive coordinated action across multiple enforcement points.
Securing agents must itself become agentic, while remaining inside boundaries people set.

extraction.body: Agents are rapidly becoming part of how work gets done. They can support a range of activities from writing code and researching products to analyzing revenue, processing expenses, and acting across the systems that run the business. To be most useful, they often need access to company data, applications, tools, and other agents. That access is what makes agents more capable. With that capability can come insider risk. This does not mean agents are inherently malicious. It means they are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems by users. They can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised. Their models can produce variable outputs, their context can change, and their plans can evolve as they work. An agent that operates as intended when a task begins may respond differently as context or inputs change. Depending on how they are designed and deployed, agents can operate continuously, at machine speed and scale. Satya Nadella, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Microsoft, recently described the trust architecture this new era requires: we must separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. We should not ask a model to be its own security authority. The controls that determine what it can access, what actions it can take, and whether it should continue operating must sit outside the model, where the model cannot bypass or tamper with them. “The most trustworthy agentic system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one designed that enables us to trust the model least.” We introduced Project Perception and the Microsoft cyber stack to help organizations defend with agents. Today, we are extending Perception to secure the agentic insider . Guardian Agents help security teams operate continuously, at machine speed and scale, while sensors, context, and actuators across the cyber stack help understand changing agent risk and continuously adapt protection in response. Project Perception and Microsoft Agent 365 share signals, context, and a unified registry giving IT and security teams a consistent view of agents and risk, with the controls each needs. This builds on a simple security principle: surround non-deterministic intelligence with deterministic controls, independent evidence, and containment boundaries. Assume an agent can fail or be compromised. Observe it continuously. Minimize and tailor its authority before it acts. And continuously adjust that authority as risk changes. This requires protection across identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud, and runtime. The system has four continuous responsibilities: These are not four products or sequential phases. They operate together. Evidence changes risk. Risk changes policy. Policy changes what the agent is allowed to do. Consider an expense-approval agent. It may need to read expense submissions, check policy, and approve routine reimbursements, but it should not inherit every permission of the employee who sponsors it. Its identity, runtime, access paths, and task-scoped authority should be explicit from the start. If it later encounters a prompt injection or attempts an action outside that task, the system should respond proportionately: preserve safe reads while blocking writes, narrow the resources it can reach, require provable human approval for a consequential step, or isolate and stop the agent when the risk warrants it. This is what continuous containment looks like in practice. You cannot secure what you cannot see. Agents can be created through Microsoft platforms, integrated through partner platforms and software development kits (SDKs), or introduced locally without a central deployment process. Microsoft Security uses native integrations, connectors, and sensors across the cyber stack to discover more of the agent estate. We are expanding discovery to 35 additional types of local agents, bringing the total to 60 supported local agents , including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot. Organizations can bring these agents into a unified registry, regardless of how they were discovered, to understand ownership, activity, and risk. Discovery tells you that an agent exists. Identity gives security and governance systems a durable anchor for controlling it. Every agent should have a first-class identity distinct from the person using or sponsoring it. We are extending Microsoft Entra Agent ID with identity types for additional agent patterns, including local and previously unknown agents discovered through security sensors. This means an agent can become a policy target even when it was not originally integrated with Microsoft Security. Agent identity anchors attribution, ownership, lifecycle, risk, permissions, authorization, and policy, so the enterprise can distinguish what a person did from what an agent did on that person’s behalf. Being able to find and identify an agent is necessary, but it is just the start. We need to understand the potential impact the agent can have in the enterprise environment. The next step is to bound the agent across its runtime, its paths to tools and resources, and the authority it can exercise. The model and harness should execute inside a controlled environment rather than inherit fully-privileged access to the device. Sandboxes such as Microsoft Execution Container (MXC) provide policy-controlled access to resources the agent needs to complete its task. They also create an enforcement boundary where security controls and observability can operate outside the agent’s reach. If the agent or harness is compromised, it should not be able to disable the controls watching it. An agent should not be free to call any tool, API, Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, resource, or other agent it can find. Local and network and data controls must mediate those paths, observe the calls, and enforce enterprise policy. Controlling the destination alone is not enough. Security must also understand the content flowing into and out of the agent, including its sensitivity, provenance, and whether untrusted data may be influencing the agent’s behavior. We have spent decades applying Zero Trust and least privilege to people. Agents make those principles even more important. An agent should not automatically inherit all the standing access of its user. It should begin with no authority and receive only what it needs for the approved task, for only as long as the task requires. Least privilege reduces exposure, but it does not eliminate risk. An expense-approval agent may begin a task with the right access and then encounter a prompt injection in an external document. Its configuration has not changed, but its behavior and risk have. For human users, a delay between detection and response may be manageable. For an agent operating at machine speed, it can be the difference between containment and impact. The security system must be able to understand what changed and act before a person can manually investigate every signal. That is why we are introducing Dynamic Agent Risk and Dynamic Conditional Access for agents. The result is not a one-time score assigned at onboarding. It is a continuously updated understanding of the agent’s current risk and whether its current authority still matches that risk. The question is not simply whether the agent should run or stop. It is what the agent should be allowed to read, change, invoke, or approve at that moment. Dynamic Conditional Access extends Microsoft Entra Conditional Access for agents so a change in risk can drive coordinated action across multiple enforcement points. The response is graduated, not binary. Policy can reduce permissions, preserve reads while blocking writes, narrow the data and resources the agent can reach, restrict network paths, shorten or revoke time-bound access, or require provable human approval before a consequential action proceeds. At the highest levels of risk, it can isolate the runtime or stop execution entirely. Return to the expense agent. It begins with narrowly scoped permission to review and approve expenses within policy. When it encounters untrusted content and attempts an unrelated action, new evidence raises its Dynamic Agent Risk. Policy responds proportionately: it can preserve read access while removing the ability to approve or write, block access to sensitive resources, and require cryptographically provable human approval for a high-impact step. If the risk continues to rise, the system can isolate the runtime or stop execution. The employee remains productive. The agent is constrained without treating every risk change as a kill-switch event. As organizations deploy thousands or hundreds of thousands of agents, manually triaging every alert and coordinating every response will not scale. Securing agents must itself become agentic, while remaining inside boundaries people set. That is why we are introducing new Playbooks and a team of Guardian Agents in Project Perception. People define policy, approval boundaries, and delegation rules. Playbooks define the desired security outcome and coordinate protective actions. Guardian Agents carry out the work at machine speed, adapting as agent activity, risk, security context, and organizational policy change. Guardian Agents can help teams understand why risk changed, investigate the relevant evidence, recommend or apply containment, and use what they learn to harden policy. This is not about outsourcing judgment. People retain control over objectives and consequential decisions. The system carries the continuous work that does not scale through manual operations. Agents will only be adopted at scale if they can be trusted at scale. At Microsoft, we are already operating in a world of hundreds of thousands of agents. As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats. Those lessons directly inform the innovations we are delivering to help every organization adopt agents with confidence.” — Terrell Cox, Corporate Vice President (CVP) and Deputy Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), Customer Security, Microsoft As model transparency increases, it creates a new source of security evidence. Chain-of-thought and other model-level signals can help identify intent drift, understand whether untrusted information is influencing reasoning, and detect when an agent’s planned actions are diverging from the task it was given. We are bringing this deeper evidence into Dynamic Agent Risk, together with signals from across the cyber stack. This builds on Satya Nadella’s principle: increase transparency into the model while keeping security decisions and enforcement independent of it. Greater model transparency gives security systems deeper evidence to detect suspicious behavior and inform Dynamic Agent Risk. But the core security principle does not change: the model cannot be its own security boundary. Independent systems must observe every layer, including the model itself, and ultimately determine and enforce what the system is allowed to do. These are not separate pillars. They make the same containment architecture stronger: better evidence, stronger assurance, more accurate risk, and more effective protection. Organizations are adopting agents to serve customers better, solve problems faster, and give people more time for the work that matters most. The goal is not to make every model perfectly predictable before it can be useful. The goal is to build systems that remain secure even when the model is not. That requires a clear division of responsibility. Models supply intelligence. People and organizations retain authority. Independent controls establish identity, limit privilege, protect data, preserve evidence, and contain unsafe action. Security continuously reassesses risk and adapts protection as the agent works. You should not have to choose between innovation and safety. Corporate Vice President, Identity and Network Access, Microsoft Protect your people, data, and infrastructure with AI-powered, end-to-end security from Microsoft.

sources.title: Microsoft warns that AI Agents could become Insider Threats - Cybersecurity Insiders
passages: Microsoft , the American technology giant, has issued a warning about the potential security risks posed by artificial intelligence (AI) agents, cautioning that these tools could become insider threats within corporate networks.
The concern is not simply that AI agents can make decisions autonomously, but that they can access company applications, sensitive information and digital tools at extraordinary speed.
Such capabilities can make their activities difficult to monitor, control or stop when a security risk emerges.
In an advisory published on October 19, 2026, Microsoft highlighted the need for businesses to exercise caution over the growing use of AI agents in connected digital environments.
As organizations increasingly integrate AI into their daily operations, questions surrounding data privacy, access privileges and accountability are becoming more important.
Microsoft is not suggesting that every AI agent is malicious.
Instead, the company is urging organizations to recognize that an agent could behave unexpectedly or become compromised.
One major concern is that these systems may be granted broader permissions than necessary to perform their assigned tasks.
Excessive access can allow an agent to move beyond its intended responsibilities and potentially bypass established security safeguards.
Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella has emphasized the importance of distinguishing between the intelligence provided to AI systems and the autonomous actions they are permitted to take.
This distinction is central to building safer AI environments.
Giving an agent advanced reasoning capabilities does not necessarily mean it should receive unrestricted access to corporate resources or the authority to execute every action independently.

AI agents offer significant opportunities for productivity, but their deployment must be accompanied by strong security controls to ensure that automation remains beneficial rather than becoming an unexpected source of organizational risk.
