extraction.body: Memphis leaders are set to consider a contentious plan Tuesday to pause new data center developments for up to a year — two weeks after a meeting on the issue led to protests, calls to police and a fist fight at City Hall. The moratorium vote comes more than two years after some communities in Memphis got a new life courtesy of trillionaire Elon Musk, as his artificial intelligence company moved in amid a local effort to make the city a hotspot for advanced technology. But the effort ended up angering residents as the company installed dozens of gas-powered turbines, known to produce a cocktail of toxic pollutants. A surge of new data center construction to fuel the booming AI industry is escalating public resentment and fear of both the energy-sucking infrastructure and AI itself in the US, roiling communities from coast to coast and transforming localized energy debates into a high-stakes, multi-million-dollar battleground for the 2026 midterm elections. At an early October council meeting in Memphis — a city used to fighting for clean air as the home to more than a dozen polluting facilities — fierce opposition was on full display. More than 100 people filed into the chamber to hear about the moratorium, bearing witness to clashes between anti-data center protesters and council members, and between the city officials themselves. All eyes will be on City Hall as it considers the moratorium, which, if passed, would put a temporary pause on new data centers and on the expansion of existing ones, as well as develop a study committee to establish regulations. It would not shutter data centers already operating legally in Memphis, nor smaller data usages at facilities like hospitals and universities. Here’s what we know: How Memphis got here An abandoned factory in southwest Memphis got a makeover in June 2024, as the AI company owned by the world’s richest man, now called SpaceXAI, worked to turn the building into the “world’s largest supercomputer.” Dubbed “Colossus,” the data center was hailed by Musk at the time as the “most powerful AI training system in the world,” and the company’s website heralded plans for a second facility in the area to quickly follow. For some residents in the southwest Memphis suburb of Boxtown, a historic, majority Black and economically disadvantaged community that has long endured industrial pollution, the new gas-powered turbines represented yet another threat to their health. The NAACP filed a federal lawsuit against SpaceXAI in April of this year under the Clean Air Act, alleging it was operating dozens of unpermitted turbines in Southaven. The Department of Justice has since urged the court to throw out the lawsuit, saying the Grok AI chatbot was “critical” to national security. The data centers have also caused a myriad of disruptions to daily life in Memphis, including relentless noise pollution and physical vibrations from the centers as described in a noise complaint filed by residents; concerns of dangerous emissions from the turbines brought by state officials; and an offer from SpaceXAI to buy Southaven residents’ homes in exchange for not signing onto a class action lawsuit against it. But it was at an August meeting — where the moratorium passed its first reading — that Memphis City Council Member JB Smiley Jr. said he proposed the measure to temporarily halt new data center builds after learning Musk’s company was planning a data center expansion in the city from a post on social media. “Not only did the council not know about the expansion of the data center, the community residents did not know,” Smiley said at the meeting. “I was intentional about bringing this ordinance because I think the people deserve an opportunity to voice their concerns; I think the council deserves to be treated with respect by the folks who are pushing these data centers in our community.” An earlier council meeting on data centers devolved into chaos Members of the Memphis City Council voted on whether to delay making a decision on the moratorium for two weeks at an October 6 meeting. When the effort to delay passed 7-5, the chamber erupted. “Officers, we need to clear it out,” council Chairwoman Jana Swearengen-Washington said from the podium as observers began shouting. As people rose from their seats in the chamber and a woman shouted chants into a megaphone speaker, the chairwoman repeatedly slammed her gavel, saying, “Get that f**king bullhorn!” A livestream of the meeting showed dozens of protesters gathering at the front of the room, fists in the air as they chanted above the council members’ shouts to stop, yelling, “Ain’t no power like the power of the people ‘cause the power of the people fight back!” before the livestream went dark. Councilwoman Yolanda Cooper-Sutton clashed with members of the crowd, according to CNN affiliate WMC, as she told one attendee, “You pipe down baby, I clap back.” She also lashed out at Smiley, who voted against postponing the vote on his moratorium, shouting that he “confuse(s) the people over and over,” as she was ushered out of the room by staffers. In the lobby of the building, a fist fight broke out between two women, WMC reported. Memphis police were called to the disturbance at City Hall, but according to WMC, a department spokesperson said no one was harmed or detained. Days after the chaotic meeting, Memphis Mayor Paul Young issued an executive order to establish a 90-day study “to develop clear, actionable recommendations for regulating large and hyperscale data centers in Memphis.” “The study will proceed concurrently with the Memphis City Council’s ongoing consideration of data center legislation,” the mayor’s office wrote in a press release. “The executive order does not suspend, delay, restrict, or interfere with Council action.” State lawmaker, among four others, banned from Tuesday’s meeting In a First Amendment lawsuit filed last week, state Rep. Pearson, along with four other people, said they were banned from attending Tuesday’s City Council meeting after opposing AI data centers at the October 6 meeting and asked for a temporary restraining order to block the ban imposed on them. In separate letters addressed to the individuals stating that they have been banned from the upcoming October 20 and November 10 sessions — all signed by Swearengen-Washington, according to documents filed — the council cited alleged violations of its decorum policy, which prohibits speech including “gossip,” personal attacks and abusive or vulgar language. The plaintiffs said those terms are vague, and that the council selectively used them to silence prominent critics, violating their First Amendment rights. “Each of the banned Plaintiffs is an active community leader and well-known activist in Memphis who was targeted because of their consistent and sustained advocacy and leadership in the fight against AI data centers, not because of any disruptive behavior,” the lawsuit says. CNN has reached out to chairwoman Swearengen-Washington and the City of Memphis. Wade, an attorney for the city and the chairwoman, declined to comment on the lawsuit, citing pending litigation. Tuesday’s meeting will feature enhanced security measures as a result of the chaos earlier this month, court documents show. The chairwoman’s office on Monday issued a new security plan for council meetings “following the events of October 6,” which include security inspections of the committee room and chambers before meetings, a relocation of the public speaking podium away from the chamber floor, along with a new clear bag policy and more restricted building access to non-city employees, according to court filings. Referendum on data centers nationwide As thousands of new data centers have been built to feed the power-hungry artificial intelligence industry, public resentment against the energy-intensive infrastructure and AI itself is escalating, plunging small towns and suburban communities from coast to coast into uncertainty and a growing national debate. Many Republican and Democratic politicians have pivoted away from backing data centers ahead of the midterms, but others — namely President Donald Trump — have doubled down on their development. Police have been called into action to investigate dozens of threats to data centers, from bomb claims etched on bathroom walls to online incitements to “use bullets on city council members” to suggestions that protesters should “unalive” pro-development officials, according to a CNN review of more than 100 police reports filed since last year. Communities are also taking their concerns with data centers into polling booths this fall, with the politics of data centers emerging as the 2026 midterms’ unlikely villain.

The moratorium vote comes more than two years after some communities in Memphis got a new life courtesy of trillionaire Elon Musk, as his artificial intelligence company moved in amid a local effort to make the city a hotspot for advanced technology.

Here’s what we know: How Memphis got here An abandoned factory in southwest Memphis got a makeover in June 2024, as the AI company owned by the world’s richest man, now called SpaceXAI, worked to turn the building into the “world’s largest supercomputer.” Dubbed “Colossus,” the data center was hailed by Musk at the time as the “most powerful AI training system in the world,” and the company’s website heralded plans for a second facility in the area to quickly follow.

The data centers have also caused a myriad of disruptions to daily life in Memphis, including relentless noise pollution and physical vibrations from the centers as described in a noise complaint filed by residents; concerns of dangerous emissions from the turbines brought by state officials; and an offer from SpaceXAI to buy Southaven residents’ homes in exchange for not signing onto a class action lawsuit against it.

City Councilwoman Yolanda Cooper-Sutton has also been suspended from her committee chairwoman duties for the next 30 days as a result of her outbursts during the meeting.
City hall security supervisors met with Memphis Police Chief CJ Davis, the commanders from the Main Street precinct and Phelps Security to develop the final plan.

extraction.body: MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - New security measures are in place ahead of Tuesday’s Memphis City Council meeting, two weeks after a council vote on a data center moratorium was delayed amid chaos in the chambers. A federal judge has a copy of the security plan while deciding whether to allow citizens banned from council meetings back into the building. Anyone attending the meeting must check in through the front doors on Main Street at City Hall. Backpacks and purses are not allowed. Under the new rules, everyone must use a clear bag. Security will inspect committee rooms and chambers before meetings. The public speaking podium in the chamber will move behind the gates near council employees, and will now face the audience. Attendance will be limited, as determined by the fire marshal. The council also has a new emergency evacuation procedure directing them to exit using specific doors, and to remain sheltered in place together until security tells them otherwise. No bullhorns or noisemakers will be allowed inside council chambers. The changes follow the October 6 meeting which ended prematurely and in great pandemonium, with Memphis City Council Chairwoman Janna Swearengen-Washington banning six citizens from the next few meetings, including state Rep. Justin J. Pearson . City Councilwoman Yolanda Cooper-Sutton has also been suspended from her committee chairwoman duties for the next 30 days as a result of her outbursts during the meeting. Yoland Cooper Sutton new filing (1).pdf by Jacob Gallant Rep. Pearson and the others fought in federal court on Monday to have the ban lifted. The council attorney, Allan Wade, submitted the new security plan to the judge handling the case. The council’s Chief Administrative Officer Takeyshia Johnson wrote in an email about the security changes, “Staff members have received threats, endured concerning phone calls and expressed concern about their physical safety and emotional well-being.” She said the changes were made after staff surveys were conducted. City hall security supervisors met with Memphis Police Chief CJ Davis, the commanders from the Main Street precinct and Phelps Security to develop the final plan. Council members are preparing to deal with five ordinances and a resolution all pertaining to data centers, including a 12-month moratorium. A vote on the moratorium was pushed back at the Oct. 6 meeting, sparking outrage from activists, leading to the disruption that ended in the clearing of council chambers and an abrupt end to that meeting. Memphis Mayor Paul Young addressed the data center drama, telling Action News 5: “When you look at the five or six or six ordinances that have been proposed by city council, one thing they all have in common, they want to determine what the guardrails are.” He added, “Irrespective of what happens tomorrow, we’re going to keep doing the work because the public has asked for it and I think they deserve it.” Read the full enhanced council security plan below: Kimberly Owens-Pearson PACER complaint 3 .pdf by Jacob Gallant

extraction.body: In seconds, her financial security vanished behind a screen inside a gas station. Thousands of dollars deposited into a cryptocurrency ATM, in what one Johnston County woman thought was a payment to law enforcement for her safe release. But when the callers – impersonating local law enforcement – on the other end of the line requested an additional $4,000, she told them she simply didn’t have the money. That’s when the call dropped, and she realized she had been depleted of what she says was the entirety of her savings. “I just set up an appointment with a counselor, so I'd have somebody to talk to, because it's really hurt me financially and hurt me mentally." This victim, who wished to share her story with WRAL but not to be identified, is among thousands of victims across the country taken advantage of via a cryptocurrency kiosk. Public records out of Harnett County show a man recently lost more than $30,000 – which was described as 'almost all' of his savings – to a cryptocurrency machine. The machines – which upon first glance resemble regular ATMs – convert deposited cash into cryptocurrency investments. Rise of cryptocurrency crimes, and how kiosks can play a role Internet crimes facilitated through cryptocurrency kiosks are rising, following similar trends with general cryptocurrency related crimes. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) began publicly reporting cryptocurrency kiosk metrics as of 2023. That year, the FBI received 5,500 complaints related to cryptocurrency kiosks, with losses of more than $189 million. Those numbers jumped in 2025, with the agency reporting 13,460 complaints totaling $389 million in victim losses. "Fraud losses at BTMs [Bitcoin ATMs] are skyrocketing, increasing nearly tenfold from 2020 to 2023," according to data cited from the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) Consumer Sentinel Network. States are upping regulations, oversight over crypto ATMs. Many states are enacting tighter consumer regulations around cryptocurrency kiosks, including several who have imposed some kind of ban altogether. This year, North Carolina state lawmakers approved several regulatory changes to the Bitcoin ATM (BTM) industry by passing House Bill 920, introduced by State Rep. Jackson Some of the bill's language includes: Requiring licenses for all kiosk operators under the Money Transmissions Act. It stipulates that kiosk operators shall refund the "full dollar amount deposited" under certain conditions, including when someone reports a "fraudulent" transmission within 30 days. Although the bill's changes go into effect in 2027, Jackson questions – based on the level of fraud cases he's seen from this technology – if there is a legitimate reason to have any in the state in the first place. You don't have to do that through a gas station. There is no reason to go to one of these machines," he told WRAL. "Only a tiny percentage of those transactions are fraud," Tente told WRAL via email. Crypto deployers are highly unlikely to operate under such rules." State Rep. Tim Longest, D-Wake, previously expressed concern to WRAL about having the kiosks at all in the state. Longest, a consumer protection lawyer, said the bill's protections could have been stronger. "I think that we should really question whether these regulations go far enough and if these machines really serve any legitimate purpose," Rep. "You don't go to put cash in a machine and take out a stock, and yet a stock is exactly the same kind of speculative asset that cryptocurrency is." Attorney General Jackson alluded to the DOJ currently looking into cryptocurrency kiosk companies. "Investigation underway as we speak," Jackson said. WRAL reached out to several cryptocurrency kiosk companies operating in North Carolina, requesting information on how they plan to comply with new state laws. Below are responses from Byte Federal, through founder and chief compliance officer Mark Paolillo, and Chief Executive Officer, Paul Tarantino, as well as a marketing spokesperson for CoinFlip. They say many of the protections are already in place, independently, as part of their company's policies. Byte Federal: Most of HB 920's requirements match what we already do: scam warnings, blockchain analytics, live customer service, a written anti-fraud program, and dedicated compliance staff. We have advocated for a waiting period for first-time customers because it gives time to stop a scam before any funds leave. CoinFlip: CoinFlip already provides many of the consumer protections required under North Carolina’s new cryptocurrency kiosk law, including live customer support, scam warnings, and technology that screens for suspicious digital wallets. We appreciate the leadership of Representative Jackson and the collaborative efforts of stakeholders in developing a regulatory framework that strengthens consumer protections while preserving access to legitimate financial services. Question: Does the company plan to reduce its number of North Carolina kiosks? We are optimistic that NC lawmakers can see the error in the fee cap and make adjustments that allow legitimate kiosk operators to do business in the state.

This year, North Carolina state lawmakers approved several regulatory changes to the Bitcoin ATM (BTM) industry by passing House Bill 920, introduced by State Rep. Neal Jackson (R). "HB920 aims to protect North Carolinians from fraud through appropriate regulatory oversight while preserving our citizens ability to manage their finances. passages: In seconds, her financial security vanished behind a screen inside a gas station.

Thousands of dollars deposited into a cryptocurrency ATM, in what one Johnston County woman thought was a payment to law enforcement for her safe release. But when the callers – impersonating local law enforcement – on the other end of the line requested an additional $4,000, she told them she simply didn’t have the money.
That’s when the call dropped, and she realized she had been depleted of what she says was the entirety of her savings.
“I just set up an appointment with a counselor, so I'd have somebody to talk to, because it's really hurt me financially and hurt me mentally."

This victim, who wished to share her story with WRAL but not to be identified, is among thousands of victims across the country taken advantage of via a cryptocurrency kiosk. Public records out of Harnett County show a man recently lost more than $30,000 – which was described as 'almost all' of his savings – to a cryptocurrency machine.

The machines – which upon first glance resemble regular ATMs – convert deposited cash into cryptocurrency investments. The transactions are virtually instant, difficult to trace and can be difficult to reverse.
Internet crimes facilitated through cryptocurrency kiosks are rising, following similar trends with general cryptocurrency related crimes.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) began publicly reporting cryptocurrency kiosk metrics as of 2023. That year, the FBI received 5,500 complaints related to cryptocurrency kiosks, with losses of more than $189 million. Those numbers jumped in 2025, with the agency reporting 13,460 complaints totaling $389 million in victim losses.
"Fraud losses at BTMs [Bitcoin ATMs] are skyrocketing, increasing nearly tenfold from 2020 to 2023," according to data cited from the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) Consumer Sentinel Network.
Many states are enacting tighter consumer regulations around cryptocurrency kiosks, including several who have imposed some kind of ban altogether.
This year, North Carolina state lawmakers approved several regulatory changes to the Bitcoin ATM (BTM) industry by passing House Bill 920, introduced by State Rep. Neal Jackson (R).

"HB920 aims to protect North Carolinians from fraud through appropriate regulatory oversight while preserving our citizens ability to manage their finances. As technology advances, this legislation embraces innovation while ensuring consumers have the protections they deserve," says Rep. Jackson

It stipulates that kiosk operators shall refund the "full dollar amount deposited" under certain conditions, including when someone reports a "fraudulent" transmission within 30 days. In an effort to reduce fraud, the bill also seeks to place limitations on transaction amounts, capping new customers at $2,000 daily for the first 30 days, and after that, at $5,000.

North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson believes the new customer limit may be the bill's most significant addition to protecting consumers. Although the bill's changes go into effect in 2027, Jackson questions – based on the level of fraud cases he's seen from this technology – if there is a legitimate reason to have any in the state in the first place.

"We don't think there is any legitimate use for these devices. They are overwhelmingly used for fraud. If you want to invest in Bitcoin, you can do that without paying the 12% overhead. You don't have to do that through a gas station. If you want to send money to somebody, you can do that through a bank. There is no reason to go to one of these machines," he told WRAL.
David Tente, the executive director of the ATM Industry Association, pushed back on Attorney General Jackson's assessment of how frequently the kiosks are used to facilitate crimes.

"Only a tiny percentage of those transactions are fraud," Tente told WRAL via email. "Many of the [bill] requirements are similar to the bill Congress is working on. However, the 30-day return requirement makes everything else rather pointless. Crypto deployers are highly unlikely to operate under such rules."

State Rep. Tim Longest, D-Wake, previously expressed concern to WRAL about having the kiosks at all in the state. Rep. Longest, a consumer protection lawyer, said the bill's protections could have been stronger.

"I think that we should really question whether these regulations go far enough and if these machines really serve any legitimate purpose," Rep. Longest said. "You don't go to put cash in a machine and take out a stock, and yet a stock is exactly the same kind of speculative asset that cryptocurrency is."
Attorney General Jackson alluded to the DOJ currently looking into cryptocurrency kiosk companies.
"Investigation underway as we speak," Jackson said.
WRAL reached out to several cryptocurrency kiosk companies operating in North Carolina, requesting information on how they plan to comply with new state laws.

Below are responses from Byte Federal, through founder and chief compliance officer Mark Paolillo, and Chief Executive Officer, Paul Tarantino, as well as a marketing spokesperson for CoinFlip. They say many of the protections are already in place, independently, as part of their company's policies.

extraction.body: In seconds, her financial security vanished behind a screen inside a gas station. Thousands of dollars deposited into a cryptocurrency ATM, in what one Johnston County woman thought was a payment to law enforcement for her safe release. But when the callers – impersonating local law enforcement – on the other end of the line requested an additional $4,000, she told them she simply didn’t have the money. That’s when the call dropped, and she realized she had been depleted of what she says was the entirety of her savings. “I just set up an appointment with a counselor, so I'd have somebody to talk to, because it's really hurt me financially and hurt me mentally." This victim, who wished to share her story with WRAL but not to be identified, is among thousands of victims across the country taken advantage of via a cryptocurrency kiosk. Public records out of Harnett County show a man recently lost more than $30,000 – which was described as 'almost all' of his savings – to a cryptocurrency machine. The machines – which upon first glance resemble regular ATMs – convert deposited cash into cryptocurrency investments. The transactions are virtually instant, difficult to trace and can be difficult to reverse. Internet crimes facilitated through cryptocurrency kiosks are rising, following similar trends with general cryptocurrency related crimes. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) began publicly reporting cryptocurrency kiosk metrics as of 2023. That year, the FBI received 5,500 complaints related to cryptocurrency kiosks, with losses of more than $189 million. Those numbers jumped in 2025, with the agency reporting 13,460 complaints totaling $389 million in victim losses. "Fraud losses at BTMs [Bitcoin ATMs] are skyrocketing, increasing nearly tenfold from 2020 to 2023," according to data cited from the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) Consumer Sentinel Network. Many states are enacting tighter consumer regulations around cryptocurrency kiosks, including several who have imposed some kind of ban altogether. This year, North Carolina state lawmakers approved several regulatory changes to the Bitcoin ATM (BTM) industry by passing House Bill 920, introduced by State Rep. Neal Jackson (R). "HB920 aims to protect North Carolinians from fraud through appropriate regulatory oversight while preserving our citizens ability to manage their finances. As technology advances, this legislation embraces innovation while ensuring consumers have the protections they deserve," says Rep. Jackson It stipulates that kiosk operators shall refund the "full dollar amount deposited" under certain conditions, including when someone reports a "fraudulent" transmission within 30 days. In an effort to reduce fraud, the bill also seeks to place limitations on transaction amounts, capping new customers at $2,000 daily for the first 30 days, and after that, at $5,000. North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson believes the new customer limit may be the bill's most significant addition to protecting consumers. Although the bill's changes go into effect in 2027, Jackson questions – based on the level of fraud cases he's seen from this technology – if there is a legitimate reason to have any in the state in the first place. "We don't think there is any legitimate use for these devices. They are overwhelmingly used for fraud. If you want to invest in Bitcoin, you can do that without paying the 12% overhead. You don't have to do that through a gas station. If you want to send money to somebody, you can do that through a bank. There is no reason to go to one of these machines," he told WRAL. David Tente, the executive director of the ATM Industry Association, pushed back on Attorney General Jackson's assessment of how frequently the kiosks are used to facilitate crimes. "Only a tiny percentage of those transactions are fraud," Tente told WRAL via email. "Many of the [bill] requirements are similar to the bill Congress is working on. However, the 30-day return requirement makes everything else rather pointless. Crypto deployers are highly unlikely to operate under such rules." State Rep. Tim Longest, D-Wake, previously expressed concern to WRAL about having the kiosks at all in the state. Rep. Longest, a consumer protection lawyer, said the bill's protections could have been stronger. "I think that we should really question whether these regulations go far enough and if these machines really serve any legitimate purpose," Rep. Longest said. "You don't go to put cash in a machine and take out a stock, and yet a stock is exactly the same kind of speculative asset that cryptocurrency is." Attorney General Jackson alluded to the DOJ currently looking into cryptocurrency kiosk companies. "Investigation underway as we speak," Jackson said. WRAL reached out to several cryptocurrency kiosk companies operating in North Carolina, requesting information on how they plan to comply with new state laws. Below are responses from Byte Federal, through founder and chief compliance officer Mark Paolillo, and Chief Executive Officer, Paul Tarantino, as well as a marketing spokesperson for CoinFlip. They say many of the protections are already in place, independently, as part of their company's policies. Answers to questions are published in full for accuracy. Question: Which HB 920 changes will require you to update your kiosks? Byte Federal: Most of HB 920's requirements match what we already do: scam warnings, blockchain analytics, live customer service, a written anti-fraud program, and dedicated compliance staff. The changes we are implementing before January 1, 2027 include: CoinFlip: CoinFlip already provides many of the consumer protections required under North Carolina’s new cryptocurrency kiosk law, including live customer support, scam warnings, and technology that screens for suspicious digital wallets. We appreciate the leadership of Representative Jackson and the collaborative efforts of stakeholders in developing a regulatory framework that strengthens consumer protections while preserving access to legitimate financial services. CoinFlip has held a North Carolina money transmitter license since May 2024 and supports clear, consistent rules and accountability for all operators. We will implement the changes necessary to comply with the law’s requirements for when they take effect. Question: Does the company plan to reduce its number of North Carolina kiosks? Byte Federal: Complying with NC regulation is an easy lift for Byte Federal because we already meet the same standards in other states. The problem is the 12% fee cap, a regulation that puts legitimate operators running full compliance out of business in NC. We are optimistic that NC lawmakers can see the error in the fee cap and make adjustments that allow legitimate kiosk operators to do business in the state. CoinFlip: CoinFlip currently operates 152 kiosks across the state and has no plans to reduce its North Carolina kiosk network as a result of the new law.” Question: What is your policy for refunding scam victims? Byte Federal: We will comply fully with HB 920's refund provisions. Under the law, when the Commissioner of Banks determines a transaction was fraudulent and the victim reported it within 30 days, new customers receive a full refund and existing customers receive a refund of fees. That said, we believe the refund mandate holds compliant kiosk operators to a standard no other part of the financial system is held to. Byte Federal operates under the same federal framework as banks and other money transmitters: the Bank Secrecy Act, the USA PATRIOT Act's customer identification and due diligence rules, OFAC sanctions screening, and the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act's privacy and data-security requirements. Yet when a bank customer is tricked into sending a wire to a scammer, the bank generally does not refund that loss. Federal consumer protection rules for electronic transfers do not cover wire transfers. Wires instead fall under Article 4A of the Uniform Commercial Code, which relieves a bank of any refund obligation when it processed the customer's payment in good faith and followed agreed security procedures. Courts have applied this to scam victims directly. In one 2024 federal case, a customer who wired money to fraudulent crypto companies could not recover it from the bank, because the customer had authorized the wires and the bank had followed its procedures. A bitcoin transaction is just as irreversible as a wire. When a customer has passed identity verification, read our scam warnings, completed a verification call if they are 60 or older, and attested that they are sending funds to their own wallet without anyone directing them, we do not believe a compliant operator should be treated differently from a bank. The money in a kiosk is not the operators to give back, and the person responsible for the loss is the criminal who stole it. More broadly, we believe the most effective protection is stopping a scam before any money is sent. Once bitcoin is sent, it cannot be recalled by us or anyone else. That is why our program focuses on the moments before a transaction: the 60+ verification calls, attestations, wallet screening, and now the 48-hour new-customer hold, during which funds can still be returned. Outside the framework established by state law, we provide refunds where Byte Federal failed to follow its required compliance procedures. We also cooperate with law enforcement on every fraud report and provide transaction and wallet data to help trace and recover funds. CoinFlip: Our current policy provides transaction-fee refunds to confirmed scam victims. Identifying and stopping suspected scams before funds are transferred is critical when we hold a transaction before a transfer is complete; we can return it to the principal. Refund requests and reported scams are evaluated case by case, and our live support team helps customers report scams and request refunds. When a scam is reported, CoinFlip works with law enforcement to help stop or track scammers. Because blockchain transactions create a public record, investigators may be able to trace funds and, in some cases, assist with recovery. CoinFlip also blocks suspicious transactions and permanently blacklists high-risk digital wallet addresses, so they cannot be used at a CoinFlip kiosk again. We will honor the additional refund rights established by North Carolina’s new law when it takes effect.”

There have been looming question marks about artificial intelligence (AI) stocks of late, and whether a bubble may be bursting. AI stocks have been struggling recently as the market worries about how much longer the strong results may last. One top tech company, however, says that it's already seeing interest for orders years in advance, due to the need for AI chips. That company is ASML Holding (NASDAQ:ASML), whose lithography machines are essential in the manufacturing process for advanced chips. ASML posted its latest earnings numbers, which not only showed that it's been growing well of late, but also that demand remains robust for a long time, and that customers are placing orders years in advance. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » The big question, however, is whether the tech stock is still a good buy given its high valuation. I'll look to answer that below. The challenge for investors when buying a stock is that it isn't as simple as buying it because the business has done well recently. If a stock is trading at a high valuation, then the market may already be pricing in a fair bit of growth. Thus, unless there is a new development that suggests there's much more growth ahead than what was already expected, the stock itself may not necessarily rally higher or be seen as a good buy. ASML is one of the largest tech companies in the world, with a market cap of more than $630 billion, and whose growth rate exceeded 55% last quarter. It's currently trading at a price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of 40, which is significant, and at that kind of valuation, a premium has been priced in. Its forward P/E multiple, which is based on future earnings results that analysts expect from the business in the year ahead, is at 29, which also isn't low; the S&P 500 average is a little over 19 right now. The company did, however, give investors reason to remain bullish on more growth ahead, as CEO Christophe Fouquet says that AI investments are driving significant orders, and that, "In light of their demand visibility, some customers are expressing an interest in placing orders with us for 2029 and even 2030." ASML's stock may not be cheap, but the company has a dominant position in the market and a strong competitive advantage. Its lithography machines are essential in the tech sector, and that's evident with customers seeking out orders well in advance, in anticipation of demand even years ahead. Some growth is certainly priced in for ASML's stock, but with the company already seeing demand into 2030, it may well be worth trading at an even higher valuation for that kind of stability and growth. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity. While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook. David Jagielski, CPA has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends ASML. Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) and Gold are the two most recognized store-of-value assets in the world. Both are built on the promise of holding value when everything else falls, but they are moving in completely opposite directions right now. Gold is trading near $5,200 an ounce after climbing 77% over the past year, hitting an all-time high of $5,595 in January. Bitcoin on the other hand, is at $70,000 after falling 47% from its own all-time high of $126,000 set in October 2025. The conventional belief is that gold is the real store of value and Bitcoin is not due to its high level of volatility. But JPMorgan recently argued the opposite , saying Bitcoin’s volatility relative to gold has dropped to a record low and that BTC is now “more attractive than gold” as a long-term investment. The bank put a $266,000 long-term price target on Bitcoin, while acknowledging it might not happen anytime soon. So which asset is Wall Street actually betting on for the next five years? A year ago, gold was trading around $2,900 an ounce. Since then, central banks have been buying at a pace not seen in decades, with China’s central bank adding gold for 15 consecutive months and countries like India and Poland building reserves alongside it. By late January, gold had already surged past $5,000 and hit an all-time high of $5,595 on January 29. When the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28, gold jumped another 2% in a single session, from roughly $5,100 to above $5,300, as investors piled into the one asset that has always worked during wartime. Bitcoin was supposed to benefit from the same kind of uncertainty. It has a fixed supply of 21 million coins—meaning no central bank can print more of it—and its supporters have long called it “digital gold.” But when the Iran strikes hit on February 28, Bitcoin dropped from $66,000 to $63,000 in a single session while gold surged by over $200. Bitcoin ETFs have now bled roughly $3.8 billion in net outflows in 2026, with February alone marking the worst single month since these products launched in January 2024. Gold-backed ETFs moved in the opposite direction, with SPDR Gold Trust and iShares Gold Trust pulling in fresh capital as the war premium drove institutional demand for physical gold exposure. Gold is up 77% over the past 12 months while Bitcoin is down 47% from its October high and roughly 25% below where it started the year. The last time gold and Bitcoin diverged this sharply was early 2020, and Bitcoin went on to rally over 1,000% in the two years that followed—JPMorgan thinks a similar setup may be forming now. JPMorgan’s quantitative strategist, Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou, argued in a February note that Bitcoin is now more attractive than gold over the long term. His reasoning is that gold has actually gotten more volatile than Bitcoin. He also points that gold’s 77% rally came with wider and more frequent price swings, while Bitcoin’s volatility has been falling—and that the ratio between the two has dropped to about 1.5, which is a record low. If Bitcoin is now closer to gold in terms of volatility, JPMorgan argues it should also be closer in terms of how much money is invested in it. Right now, roughly $8 trillion in private sector capital sits in gold through ETFs, bars, and coins. For Bitcoin to match that level of investment, JPMorgan forecasts its price would need to reach $266,000 . On top of that, BTC is trading below its estimated production cost of $87,000—what it costs miners on average to produce one coin—and every time that’s happened in past cycles, the price eventually recovered. The bank’s own commodity team projects gold at $6,300 by year-end, which is about 21% upside from $5,200. Compare that to the 280% implied by their $266,000 Bitcoin target from current levels near $70,000, and it’s clear which asset JPMorgan thinks has more room to move. As JPMorgan argues Bitcoin is the better bet, Goldman Sachs believes otherwise. The bank raised its year-end gold price target to $5,400 per ounce in January, which from $5,200 today still implies upside with room to run further as central banks keep buying. Goldman’s reasoning is that central banks are still buying gold at a pace not seen in decades and that gold doesn’t need Bitcoin-style volatility to deliver strong returns. Gold has also never lost more than 45% of its value in a single drawdown, while Bitcoin has dropped over 50% four times since 2017 . For Goldman, the consistency is what makes gold a safer long-term hold compared to BTC. Bitcoin has more room to run from $70,000 than gold does from $5,200, but you’d have to hold through 40-50% drawdowns to get there. Gold doesn’t ask that of you. The thing is, gold has sharply outperformed Bitcoin before, in 2015 and again in early 2020, and both times Bitcoin eventually caught up and blew past it—and the same type of gap is forming now. Moreso, Bitcoin now has an institutional foundation that didn’t exist during previous drawdowns, with spot ETFs holding over $100 billion in assets and Strategy alone sitting on 738,000 BTC. If the institutional floor is strong enough to drive a recovery once the macro pressure eases, buying Bitcoin at $70,000 with JPMorgan’s $266,000 long-term target on the table could end up being one of the better entry points of this cycle. JPMorgan’s quantitative strategist, Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou, argued in a February note that Bitcoin is now more attractive than gold over the long term. His reasoning is that gold has actually gotten more volatile than Bitcoin. He also points that gold’s 77% rally came with wider and more frequent price swings, while Bitcoin’s volatility has been falling—and that the ratio between the two has dropped to about 1.5, which is a record low.

If Bitcoin is now closer to gold in terms of volatility, JPMorgan argues it should also be closer in terms of how much money is invested in it. Right now, roughly $8 trillion in private sector capital sits in gold through ETFs, bars, and coins. For Bitcoin to match that level of investment, JPMorgan forecasts its price would need to reach $266,000 .

On top of that, BTC is trading below its estimated production cost of $87,000—what it costs miners on average to produce one coin—and every time that’s happened in past cycles, the price eventually recovered. The bank’s own commodity team projects gold at $6,300 by year-end, which is about 21% upside from $5,200. Compare that to the 280% implied by their $266,000 Bitcoin target from current levels near $70,000, and it’s clear which asset JPMorgan thinks has more room to move.

As JPMorgan argues Bitcoin is the better bet, Goldman Sachs believes otherwise. The bank raised its year-end gold price target to $5,400 per ounce in January, which from $5,200 today still implies upside with room to run further as central banks keep buying. Goldman’s reasoning is that central banks are still buying gold at a pace not seen in decades and that gold doesn’t need Bitcoin-style volatility to deliver strong returns.

Gold has also never lost more than 45% of its value in a single drawdown, while Bitcoin has dropped over 50% four times since 2017 . For Goldman, the consistency is what makes gold a safer long-term hold compared to BTC.

Bitcoin has more room to run from $70,000 than gold does from $5,200, but you’d have to hold through 40-50% drawdowns to get there. Gold doesn’t ask that of you. The thing is, gold has sharply outperformed Bitcoin before, in 2015 and again in early 2020, and both times Bitcoin eventually caught up and blew past it—and the same type of gap is forming now.

Moreso, Bitcoin now has an institutional foundation that didn’t exist during previous drawdowns, with spot ETFs holding over $100 billion in assets and Strategy alone sitting on 738,000 BTC. If the institutional floor is strong enough to drive a recovery once the macro pressure eases, buying Bitcoin at $70,000 with JPMorgan’s $266,000 long-term target on the table could end up being one of the better entry points of this cycle. If not, gold at $5,200 with JPMorgan projecting $6,300 to $8,000 and central banks still loading up was the right call all along.

Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) and Gold are the two most recognized store-of-value assets in the world. Both are built on the promise of holding value when everything else falls, but they are moving in completely opposite directions right now. Gold is trading near $5,200 an ounce after climbing 77% over the past year, hitting an all-time high of $5,595 in January. Bitcoin on the other hand, is at $70,000 after falling 47% from its own all-time high of $126,000 set in October 2025. The conventional belief is that gold is the real store of value and Bitcoin is not due to its high level of volatility. But JPMorgan recently argued the opposite , saying Bitcoin’s volatility relative to gold has dropped to a record low and that BTC is now “more attractive than gold” as a long-term investment. The bank put a $266,000 long-term price target on Bitcoin, while acknowledging it might not happen anytime soon. So which asset is Wall Street actually betting on for the next five years? A year ago, gold was trading around $2,900 an ounce. Since then, central banks have been buying at a pace not seen in decades, with China’s central bank adding gold for 15 consecutive months and countries like India and Poland building reserves alongside it. By late January, gold had already surged past $5,000 and hit an all-time high of $5,595 on January 29. When the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28, gold jumped another 2% in a single session, from roughly $5,100 to above $5,300, as investors piled into the one asset that has always worked during wartime. Bitcoin was supposed to benefit from the same kind of uncertainty. It has a fixed supply of 21 million coins—meaning no central bank can print more of it—and its supporters have long called it “digital gold.” But when the Iran strikes hit on February 28, Bitcoin dropped from $66,000 to $63,000 in a single session while gold surged by over $200. Bitcoin ETFs have now bled roughly $3.8 billion in net outflows in 2026, with February alone marking the worst single month since these products launched in January 2024. Gold-backed ETFs moved in the opposite direction, with SPDR Gold Trust and iShares Gold Trust pulling in fresh capital as the war premium drove institutional demand for physical gold exposure. Gold is up 77% over the past 12 months while Bitcoin is down 47% from its October high and roughly 25% below where it started the year. The last time gold and Bitcoin diverged this sharply was early 2020, and Bitcoin went on to rally over 1,000% in the two years that followed—JPMorgan thinks a similar setup may be forming now. JPMorgan’s quantitative strategist, Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou, argued in a February note that Bitcoin is now more attractive than gold over the long term. His reasoning is that gold has actually gotten more volatile than Bitcoin. He also points that gold’s 77% rally came with wider and more frequent price swings, while Bitcoin’s volatility has been falling—and that the ratio between the two has dropped to about 1.5, which is a record low. If Bitcoin is now closer to gold in terms of volatility, JPMorgan argues it should also be closer in terms of how much money is invested in it. Right now, roughly $8 trillion in private sector capital sits in gold through ETFs, bars, and coins. For Bitcoin to match that level of investment, JPMorgan forecasts its price would need to reach $266,000 . On top of that, BTC is trading below its estimated production cost of $87,000—what it costs miners on average to produce one coin—and every time that’s happened in past cycles, the price eventually recovered. The bank’s own commodity team projects gold at $6,300 by year-end, which is about 21% upside from $5,200. Compare that to the 280% implied by their $266,000 Bitcoin target from current levels near $70,000, and it’s clear which asset JPMorgan thinks has more room to move. As JPMorgan argues Bitcoin is the better bet, Goldman Sachs believes otherwise. The bank raised its year-end gold price target to $5,400 per ounce in January, which from $5,200 today still implies upside with room to run further as central banks keep buying. Goldman’s reasoning is that central banks are still buying gold at a pace not seen in decades and that gold doesn’t need Bitcoin-style volatility to deliver strong returns. Gold has also never lost more than 45% of its value in a single drawdown, while Bitcoin has dropped over 50% four times since 2017 . For Goldman, the consistency is what makes gold a safer long-term hold compared to BTC. Bitcoin has more room to run from $70,000 than gold does from $5,200, but you’d have to hold through 40-50% drawdowns to get there. Gold doesn’t ask that of you. The thing is, gold has sharply outperformed Bitcoin before, in 2015 and again in early 2020, and both times Bitcoin eventually caught up and blew past it—and the same type of gap is forming now. Moreso, Bitcoin now has an institutional foundation that didn’t exist during previous drawdowns, with spot ETFs holding over $100 billion in assets and Strategy alone sitting on 738,000 BTC. If the institutional floor is strong enough to drive a recovery once the macro pressure eases, buying Bitcoin at $70,000 with JPMorgan’s $266,000 long-term target on the table could end up being one of the better entry points of this cycle. Since then, central banks have been buying at a pace not seen in decades, with China’s central bank adding gold for 15 consecutive months and countries like India and Poland building reserves alongside it. By late January, gold had already surged past $5,000 and hit an all-time high of $5,595 on January 29. When the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28, gold jumped another 2% in a single session, from roughly $5,100 to above $5,300, as investors piled into the one asset that has always worked during wartime.

Bitcoin was supposed to benefit from the same kind of uncertainty. It has a fixed supply of 21 million coins—meaning no central bank can print more of it—and its supporters have long called it “digital gold.” But when the Iran strikes hit on February 28, Bitcoin dropped from $66,000 to $63,000 in a single session while gold surged by over $200. Bitcoin ETFs have now bled roughly $3.8 billion in net outflows in 2026, with February alone marking the worst single month since these products launched in January 2024. Gold-backed ETFs moved in the opposite direction, with SPDR Gold Trust and iShares Gold Trust pulling in fresh capital as the war premium drove institutional demand for physical gold exposure.

Gold is up 77% over the past 12 months while Bitcoin is down 47% from its October high and roughly 25% below where it started the year. The last time gold and Bitcoin diverged this sharply was early 2020, and Bitcoin went on to rally over 1,000% in the two years that followed—JPMorgan thinks a similar setup may be forming now.

JPMorgan’s quantitative strategist, Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou, argued in a February note that Bitcoin is now more attractive than gold over the long term. His reasoning is that gold has actually gotten more volatile than Bitcoin. He also points that gold’s 77% rally came with wider and more frequent price swings, while Bitcoin’s volatility has been falling—and that the ratio between the two has dropped to about 1.5, which is a record low.

If Bitcoin is now closer to gold in terms of volatility, JPMorgan argues it should also be closer in terms of how much money is invested in it. Right now, roughly $8 trillion in private sector capital sits in gold through ETFs, bars, and coins. For Bitcoin to match that level of investment, JPMorgan forecasts its price would need to reach $266,000 .

On top of that, BTC is trading below its estimated production cost of $87,000—what it costs miners on average to produce one coin—and every time that’s happened in past cycles, the price eventually recovered. The bank’s own commodity team projects gold at $6,300 by year-end, which is about 21% upside from $5,200. Compare that to the 280% implied by their $266,000 Bitcoin target from current levels near $70,000, and it’s clear which asset JPMorgan thinks has more room to move.

As JPMorgan argues Bitcoin is the better bet, Goldman Sachs believes otherwise. The bank raised its year-end gold price target to $5,400 per ounce in January, which from $5,200 today still implies upside with room to run further as central banks keep buying. Goldman’s reasoning is that central banks are still buying gold at a pace not seen in decades and that gold doesn’t need Bitcoin-style volatility to deliver strong returns.

Gold has also never lost more than 45% of its value in a single drawdown, while Bitcoin has dropped over 50% four times since 2017 . For Goldman, the consistency is what makes gold a safer long-term hold compared to BTC.

Bitcoin has more room to run from $70,000 than gold does from $5,200, but you’d have to hold through 40-50% drawdowns to get there. Gold doesn’t ask that of you. The thing is, gold has sharply outperformed Bitcoin before, in 2015 and again in early 2020, and both times Bitcoin eventually caught up and blew past it—and the same type of gap is forming now.

Moreso, Bitcoin now has an institutional foundation that didn’t exist during previous drawdowns, with spot ETFs holding over $100 billion in assets and Strategy alone sitting on 738,000 BTC. If the institutional floor is strong enough to drive a recovery once the macro pressure eases, buying Bitcoin at $70,000 with JPMorgan’s $266,000 long-term target on the table could end up being one of the better entry points of this cycle. If not, gold at $5,200 with JPMorgan projecting $6,300 to $8,000 and central banks still loading up was the right call all along.

BitMine Chairman Tom Lee says de-risking in the US, South Korea, and Taiwan is spilling into crypto markets. Ethereum (ETH), the asset BitMine holds, fell 1.91% over seven days while Bitcoin (BTC) slipped 0.177%. Lee cites AI funding and safety worries, US-Iran war activity, midterm nerves and rising bond yields as triggers. He says those pressures hit chip and memory stocks first, then the Korean and Taiwanese markets dominated by them. South Korea shows the strain most clearly. The KOSPI fell 17% in October through October 16, then dropped 3.5% at Tuesday's open. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix made up 44% of the index in May. Between October 1 and 16, they lost 19.74% and 28.38%, respectively, JoongAng Daily reported. Brokers forced out leveraged traders, with forced liquidations topping 50 billion won for four straight sessions through October 16. Taiwan held up better, with the TAIEX down 1.73% over the same October stretch. It still sank 3.41% on October 15 after September US inflation of 3.7% beat forecasts of 3.6%. Lee ties that regional selling directly to crypto. "Crypto is widely held in the US, Korea and Taiwan. So naturally, when investors in those regions de-risk, this creates spillover pressures in crypto markets," he said. Lee's own company offers one gauge of that Korean exposure. Korean investors put a net $1.4 billion into BitMine shares in 2025, according to Korea Securities Depository data. Crypto prices have moved far less than Korean stocks. At press time, Bitcoin traded at $81,385, down 1.21% in 24 hours, while ETH traded at $2,387.07, down 1.47%. Over a longer window, ETH has fallen further. It sits about 52% below its $4,946.05 peak from August 24, 2025. Bitcoin is about 35% below its $126,080 high from October 6, 2025. BitMine holds ETH as its treasury asset. Lee's buy call therefore leans partly on the laggard of the two. He still sees the drop as an opening for buyers. "In the past, whenever fundamentals remain resilient and strong, while price declines, these have historically been attractive risk/reward opportunities," he noted. His case rests on crypto's role in upgrading the plumbing of global finance. He also points to agentic AI, where software agents carry out tasks on their own. Asian markets tested that claim in August 2024. On August 5, the KOSPI plunged 8.77%, and Bitcoin sank below $50,000 for the first time since February. The next day, the KOSPI rose 3.3%, while Bitcoin briefly topped $56,000 and ETH climbed above $2,500. That quick rebound fits the pattern Lee describes. Lee's case assumes prices are falling while fundamentals hold. Dan Greenhaus of Solus Alternative Asset Management points to higher borrowing costs instead, a pressure strong fundamentals don't offset. ETH's next move hinges on whether forced selling in Seoul slows. US rates matter too, since Lee lists rising bond yields among his own triggers. That means his buy case needs rates to ease as well as fundamentals to hold. Read the Original story Is Korea's Chip Selloff a Crypto Buying Opportunity? The fundamental backdrop is cooperating here. AMD posted Q1 2026 revenue of $10.25 billion, up 38% year over year, with the Data Center segment up 57% year over year to $5.78 billion. CEO Lisa Su called it an “outstanding first quarter, driven by accelerating demand for AI infrastructure.” Broadcom’s Q2 FY2026 AI semiconductor revenue reached $10.8 billion, up 143% year over year.

Overseas action set the tone for tech stocks in general. South Korea’s SK Hynix jumped 5% in Seoul, and Samsung ripped higher after posting preliminary Q2 operating profit of roughly 89.4 trillion won, or $58.44 billion, up about 19 times year over year on revenue up 129% year over year. The selloff from earlier this week now looks like profit-taking against those numbers rather than a fundamental crack.

Two secondary tailwinds helped. President Trump said Iran called seeking a deal, easing geopolitical anxiety and lifting futures. Also, SK Hynix is set to price its U.S. IPO Thursday, refocusing investor attention on high-bandwidth memory demand tied to AI training.

Micron Technology ( NASDAQ:MU ) is riding the same wave, with MU shares up 8% in early trading to $1,027.81. Micron’s Q3 FY2026 revenue came in at $41.46 billion, and CEO Sanjay Mehrotra emphasized the “strategic value of memory in the AI era.”

NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA ) is the notable outlier, with NVDA shares down 1% to $201.92. Polymarket traders assign a 69% probability that NVIDIA closes down today, suggesting rotation into laggards like Intel and AMD rather than fresh money chasing the mega-cap leader.

The rotation story shows up in the tape. AMD stock is up 142% year to date, and INTC stock is up 199% across the same period, meaning traders are pressing recent momentum names rather than the AI incumbent.

The bear case hasn’t disappeared, though. Valuations are rich after a huge run, memory pricing remains cyclical, and Chinese competition (highlighted by DeepSeek’s reported in-house AI chip effort) keeps the long-term debate polarizing. Investors should consider keeping their position sizes measured even as share prices rise.

The SK Hynix U.S. IPO pricing this evening is the next real-time data point. A strong book would validate Lee’s structural read on memory demand and could extend the rebound into Friday. However, a soft result could stall momentum and reopen the profit-taking narrative that dominated last week.

Intraday, traders can watch for whether AMD stock holds above the $550 level into the afternoon. That level, plus the semiconductor ETF’s ability to close near its intraday high, will tell investors whether today’s bounce is the start of a new leg or another countertrend pop inside a choppier range.

BitMine Chairman Tom Lee says de-risking in the US, South Korea, and Taiwan is spilling into crypto markets. Ethereum (ETH), the asset BitMine holds, fell 1.91% over seven days while Bitcoin (BTC) slipped 0.177%. Lee cites AI funding and safety worries, US-Iran war activity, midterm nerves and rising bond yields as triggers. He says those pressures hit chip and memory stocks first, then the Korean and Taiwanese markets dominated by them. South Korea shows the strain most clearly. The KOSPI fell 17% in October through October 16, then dropped 3.5% at Tuesday's open. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix made up 44% of the index in May. Between October 1 and 16, they lost 19.74% and 28.38%, respectively, JoongAng Daily reported. Brokers forced out leveraged traders, with forced liquidations topping 50 billion won for four straight sessions through October 16. Taiwan held up better, with the TAIEX down 1.73% over the same October stretch. It still sank 3.41% on October 15 after September US inflation of 3.7% beat forecasts of 3.6%. Lee ties that regional selling directly to crypto. "Crypto is widely held in the US, Korea and Taiwan. So naturally, when investors in those regions de-risk, this creates spillover pressures in crypto markets," he said. Lee's own company offers one gauge of that Korean exposure. Korean investors put a net $1.4 billion into BitMine shares in 2025, according to Korea Securities Depository data. Crypto prices have moved far less than Korean stocks. At press time, Bitcoin traded at $81,385, down 1.21% in 24 hours, while ETH traded at $2,387.07, down 1.47%. Over a longer window, ETH has fallen further. It sits about 52% below its $4,946.05 peak from August 24, 2025. Bitcoin is about 35% below its $126,080 high from October 6, 2025. BitMine holds ETH as its treasury asset. Lee's buy call therefore leans partly on the laggard of the two. He still sees the drop as an opening for buyers. "In the past, whenever fundamentals remain resilient and strong, while price declines, these have historically been attractive risk/reward opportunities," he noted. His case rests on crypto's role in upgrading the plumbing of global finance. He also points to agentic AI, where software agents carry out tasks on their own. Asian markets tested that claim in August 2024. On August 5, the KOSPI plunged 8.77%, and Bitcoin sank below $50,000 for the first time since February. The next day, the KOSPI rose 3.3%, while Bitcoin briefly topped $56,000 and ETH climbed above $2,500. That quick rebound fits the pattern Lee describes. Lee's case assumes prices are falling while fundamentals hold. Dan Greenhaus of Solus Alternative Asset Management points to higher borrowing costs instead, a pressure strong fundamentals don't offset. ETH's next move hinges on whether forced selling in Seoul slows. US rates matter too, since Lee lists rising bond yields among his own triggers. That means his buy case needs rates to ease as well as fundamentals to hold. Read the Original story Is Korea's Chip Selloff a Crypto Buying Opportunity? South Korea’s SK Hynix jumped 5% in Seoul, and Samsung ripped higher after posting preliminary Q2 operating profit of roughly 89.4 trillion won, or $58.44 billion, up about 19 times year over year on revenue up 129% year over year. The selloff from earlier this week now looks like profit-taking against those numbers rather than a fundamental crack.

Two secondary tailwinds helped. President Trump said Iran called seeking a deal, easing geopolitical anxiety and lifting futures. Also, SK Hynix is set to price its U.S. IPO Thursday, refocusing investor attention on high-bandwidth memory demand tied to AI training.

Micron Technology ( NASDAQ:MU ) is riding the same wave, with MU shares up 8% in early trading to $1,027.81. Micron’s Q3 FY2026 revenue came in at $41.46 billion, and CEO Sanjay Mehrotra emphasized the “strategic value of memory in the AI era.”

sources.title: Microsoft says AI agents are like insider threats as ‘frontier models can’t be trusted’
passages: Project Perception was Microsoft’s answer to powerful hacking models like Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable and OpenAI’s security vulnerability scanning system Daybreak.

Project Perception originally launched three classes of agents: a “red team” that acted like hackers and attacked, a “blue team” that detected the red team and assessed the vulnerabilities they found, and a “green team” tasked with fixing them.
Microsoft was an inaugural member of Nvidia’s new Open Agent Safety Platform, which garnered the support of more than 100 other tech companies .
The platform isolates agents in secure environments and can monitor and stop behavior through hardware, functioning something like a kill switch.
“Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted,” she wrote , adding that this isn’t because they are malicious or easily hacked, but because they are unpredictable.
They have been trained to achieve tasks, not follow “organizational norms or judgment.”
Microsoft is now seizing that business opportunity in a variety of ways.

In addition to Guardian Agents, it has added an agent detection feature to its Microsoft Defender product that can find up to 60 types of agents that employees bring into the workplace, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw.
It has also added features that limit agents’ access to data and systems, and dynamically adjust their agent permissions based on the task.
That includes requiring human approval if an agent appears to be making risky decisions.

But lately, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been warning that the AI enemy may be the very agents enterprises have deployed and are paying for, much like a rogue human employee, otherwise known as an “insider threat.”
Microsoft on Monday introduced new security features designed to protect enterprises from the growing threat of AI agents.
The launch comes as Microsoft continues to warn enterprises about the dangers of AI and agents.
The surprising side is that Microsoft is famously close to OpenAI and Anthropic, having invested in both.
OpenAI is also one of its biggest cloud customers, and Microsoft has its own AI lab developing models.
Earlier this month, in his private blog , Nadella warned that it’s time to stop trusting AI model providers, even if they offer assurances of safety and security with their agentic products.
He wants enterprises to implement separate systems, not controlled by the AI labs, to watch and control the agents that those AI labs’ products launch.
But conflicting interests aside, its logic is sound.
The software that monitors agent behavior should be separate from the suppliers of agents, just as auditors should be independent of the organizations they audit.

passages: Apple tightened its developer guidelines over the weekend to ban apps that use AI to create offensive content, as well as those that masquerade as regular apps to pass the App Store review process and then turn into nudify apps, or surface those features prominently.
In July, the city of San Francisco ordered both Apple and Google to clean up and delete nudification apps from their app stores.
City Attorney David Chiu accused the companies of profiting from these apps through store fees.
And in April, a Tech Transparency Project report indicated that both tech giants’ stores hosted multiple nudify apps , some of which were rated as suitable for minors.
Apple said last year its review process blocked over 150,000 apps from reaching users and removed 193,000 developer accounts due to fraud and abuse.

The company updated its guidelines with strong language around AI and user-generated content, and how app developers should include enough preventative measures to moderate objectionable or offensive content. “Apps that host user-generated content are required to filter objectionable material, give users a way to report offensive content, and let users block abusive accounts. Apps containing hidden or undocumented features are also prohibited on the App Store, including apps that misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as ‘nudification’ — after approval, a tactic commonly known as bait-and-switch,” the company said in a blog post . extraction.body: If there’s one lesson the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident taught us, it’s that AI agents can be unpredictable. “Imagine if something like that happened in the physical world,” Howie Sun, CEO and co-founder of Laplace Intelligence , told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real world, and we don’t really want physical AI to fail in the real world.” Ann Arbor-based Laplace is building automated red-teaming — essentially, stress-testing a system by deliberately trying to make it fail — for robotics and physical AI. The company is betting that the only way to make sure physical AI is safe is to have AI test it. “Our goal is to help companies discover and fix problems before deployment — and, over time, build a shared foundation of evidence that customers, insurers, and regulators can trust,” Sun said. Laplace is one of 20 startups competing in Startup Battlefield 200, the startup pitch competition taking place at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco this week, October 13-15. It will present on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday afternoon , October 13. Sun, alongside his co-founder and chief scientist Henry Liu, founded Laplace a year ago out of the University of Michigan. Sun has spent the last eight years in academia researching how to challenge autonomous driving AI in simulation. In 2023, he and Liu — his then-PhD adviser — published a paper on the subject that made it onto the cover of the top scientific journal Nature. That’s when the calls started coming in from autonomous vehicle companies interested in implementing their ideas. “I realized that I wanted to build this and take it from purely academic research into a product that’s useful in the real world,” Sun said. Using their academic research as a base, Sun and Liu built Laplace, so named for “Laplace’s demon,” an 1814 thought experiment by French scholar Pierre-Simon Laplace, who imagined that if you knew the exact state of everything in the universe, you could predict the future with total precision. “We are essentially using simulation to predict the real world’s future,” Sun said. At the startup’s core is a high-fidelity simulation reconstructed from the real world, paired with an AI agent that constantly probes for weaknesses and failure points. The goal is to ensure that any physical AI — be it a robot, autonomous vehicle, or smart city solution — is safe in simulation before it’s deployed in the real world. The simulation environment is a post-trained version of Nvidia’s Cosmos, an AI world simulation platform, which is grounded in the real world, allowing Laplace to reconstruct anything from an Arizona highway to a Paris pedestrian crossing. Simulations are generated by blending a mesh of different real-world information. A Google Street View image could serve as a reference from which an entire street is generated. But rather than generating something random, the simulator combines real-world map data to re-create an environment that’s true to scale. Developers can then use language prompts to change the setting in real time, like adding in afternoon traffic. Sun says Laplace pulls real-time traffic and congestion information from navigation providers like TomTom. Within Laplace’s simulations, not only is the environment simulated, but also the behavior of other actors. For example, during a demo, Sun directed the test agent vehicle to swerve into oncoming traffic. The car it would have hit — or driven through, as is common among some generative world models — moved out of its way to avoid a collision. “It’s truly an interactive simulation environment,” Sun said. “Everyone is reacting to everything … This is more like a world model with interactive participants.” While the simulated environment is an important part of Laplace’s product, the real unique selling point is the AI agents the startup is developing to automatically design corner cases (tricky, rare scenarios that could trip up an AI system), moving the human further out of the loop. “They can design from the news, from police reports on collisions — all kinds of information to actively challenge the autonomous vehicles and other physical AI agents,” Sun said. Today, autonomous vehicle developers mostly train an AI to handle edge cases using recorded footage that they then turn into a simulation, or by relying on humans to come up with new ideas and design them. While many AV companies have done what Laplace is pitching and started embracing AI to create edge cases for training — self-driving truck company Waabi comes to mind — the need for this kind of technology will really become apparent when we start placing generalized robots in the real world. “There’s less data on generalized robotics,” Sun said. “No one knows what the edge cases will be in the real world.” Despite Sun and Liu coming from academia, with no shiny Silicon Valley tech company pedigrees, the two have managed to start generating revenue and even turn a modest profit. Most of the money is coming from autonomous driving use cases, with customers including Texas-based autonomous trucking firm Bot Auto and a major Japanese automotive manufacturer. Laplace is also working with Nvidia and T-Mobile on a free smart city pilot for San Jose, California, to provide high-level traffic operations. Laplace is also in the early stages of working with partners building humanoid robotics for warehouses. Most of Laplace’s customer contracts are project-based today, and the company is working toward turning that into recurring revenue. The startup’s near-term goal — which it hopes will be aided by competing at Disrupt — is to raise funds and scale so it can compete with its rivals. Chief among its rivals is Applied Intuition , a buzzy late-stage startup that’s raised $1.2 billion to date at a $15 billion post-money valuation. Sun isn’t too worried. He believes Laplace’s core methodology of using AI to test AI is a “new paradigm that changes the testing of physical AI entirely,” turning it into a “dynamic interactive testing process.” This article has been updated to clarify Laplace’s relationship with Nvidia.
